The suspect in the Banga National High School shooting incident, which killed three students in the South Cotabato town, was a Grade 9 student and the son of an employee of the Department of Education in Region 12.
Banga Mayor Albert Palencia said the shooter reportedly told his friends after lunch that they should go home. He warned them that he might do something bad.

“May isang estudyante na nagsabi sa kaibigan niya na after lunch, ‘dapat mag-uwi na kayo, kasi meron akong gagawin after lunch. Baka madamay pa kayo’. Yung mga classmate niya, nagtawa, akala niya, linoloko lang sila ng shooter,” Palencia told Super Radyo dzBB.
(There was a student that told his friends that after lunch, ‘go home, because I will do something after lunch.’ The classmates laughed, thinking that the shooter was joking.)
It was said that the student left his classroom and opened fire in the adjacent classroom.
Palencia said the shooter brought two magazines for a 9 mm gun. After he opened fire on other students, the shooter reportedly turned the gun on himself after changing magazines.
The student reportedly got the gun from his own father.
“Yung papa niya, shooter din. At saka empleyado ng DepEd Region XII. Kaya 'yung baril, tinatago sa vault, sinira ng bata 'yung vault at saka dinala 'yung baril sa eskwelahan,” Palencia said.
(His father was a shooter, also. And an employee of DepEd Region XII. So the gun was hidden in the vault, the kid broke the vault, and then he brought the gun to school.)
The mayor said he learned that the mother of the shooter was planning to take her child to seek psychiatric help.
The shooter’s sibling was also a teacher in the high school.
His father was in General Santos, teaching about child safety. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: The rise of the AfD: The all-or-nothing party
articles.summary: The AfD is riding high after its latest electoral triumph in Saxony-Anhalt. But one question remains: does the party actually want to govern?

image.caption: The AfD's election winners celebrated their victory by singing the national anthemImage: Ronny Hartmann/AFP

blocks.text: With just under 44% of the vote, the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as by far the strongest party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. It fell only narrowly short of an absolute majority in the newly elected state parliament, and with it the opportunity to govern on its own.

From the outset, the AfD made clear that governing alone was its preferred outcome. Only by avoiding having to compromise with coalition partners, the party argued, could it fully implement its agenda, which included compulsory work schemes for asylum seekers, citizen patrols monitoring migration-related issues, and the abolition of all public funding for democracy and civic engagement programs.

While Germany was debating whether the so-called "firewall" against the AfD was an appropriate means of protecting democracy, the party itself had long since built a wall of its own. For years, it has dismissed its political rivals as "cartel parties," effectively grouping them together with criminal organizations.

Teresa Haußmann of the University of Potsdam has been studying the AfD and other populist parties for years. In her view, the AfD sees "all other parties as part of a political elite that must be opposed."
After AfD's record result: Voices from Saxony-Anhalt
Ulrich Siegmund: 'No compromises!'

On election night, at the height of the celebrations, the AfD's emerging star and lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, adopted a notably more conciliatory tone than he had done throughout his campaign. "As a democrat, I extend my hand to all political forces willing to pursue a fundamental change of course with us,” he said in an interview with German public broadcaster ARD.
Moments later, however, he qualified the offer: "There will be no bending on my part, no compromises.”

Within the AfD, compromise is frequently portrayed as a sign of weakness or a betrayal of principle. According to political scientist Haußmann, this is typical of populist parties not only in Germany but in many other countries as well. "The basic premise is that a clearly identifiable popular will exists. If that is the case, then there can be only one correct political course. Any compromise would call that premise into question, because it would mean acknowledging that more than one legitimate path exists."

Little remains of the conciliatory tone struck on election night. As they did throughout the campaign, senior AfD politicians are once again targeting their political opponents with insults and inflammatory rhetoric.
Merz and Weidel clash in parliament after AfD election win
Few power-sharing options for the AfD

In fact, the parties most likely to be considered potential coalition partners are often the ones the AfD attacks most fiercely. At present, the most obvious candidates are the center-right conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the smaller left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

Immediately after the election victory, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel launched a blistering attack on the chancellor's party, declaring: "The CDU/CSU will never be able to win another federal election. That's a fact."

The Christian Democrats, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party, were the big losers of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. Some conservatives believe the party has drifted too far to the left. It is precisely those disillusioned voters that the AfD is hoping to attract.

At the same time, the AfD has adopted increasingly radical rhetoric and, in Saxony-Anhalt, is classified by the security authorities as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization. The primary reason is that the party questions the legal equality of Germans with an immigrant background.
AfD aims for destruction of opponents

Leading figures within the AfD have repeatedly described the CDU's "destruction" as a political objective. Torben Braga, a prominent lawyer, party strategist and AfD member of parliament, made the party's confrontational stance toward its political rivals clear during a panel discussion organized by the far-right publishing house Antaios. According to Braga, the AfD's goal is to become strong enough either to govern on its own or to trigger such profound upheaval within competing parties that they are effectively transformed into entirely new political forces.
The AfD thus appears to be pinning its hopes on the CDU's gradual decline, focusing on attracting disillusioned conservative voters rather than working with the party.
Why MAGA supports Germany's rise of the far-right
Could the BSW become a coalition partner?

For the moment, that leaves only one realistic partner: the relatively new Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW). The party was founded by former Left Party star Sahra Wagenknecht, who has achieved electoral success with a left-wing economic platform and a foreign policy stance widely seen as sympathetic to Russia.

For the first time, the BSW has entered the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament and could now emerge as kingmaker for the AfD. The party has signaled its openness to talks and potential cooperation. The two parties also share significant common ground on policy.

But how did the AfD respond? Shortly after its election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, the party turned its fire on the BSW. Appearing on the far-right online channel Compact TV, AfD parliamentary group leader Oliver Kirchner referred to BSW politician Fabio De Masi as a "half-Italian." He went on to suggest that the BSW could not be relied upon if problems were ever to arise within a governing partnership.

The influential AfD leader in Thuringia, Björn Höcke, dismissed the BSW as the "latest cartel party." The signals coming from the AfD point neither to a willingness to compromise nor to any desire for rapprochement. On the contrary, even without a majority of its own, the party appears determined to stay the course and pursue its radical agenda.
Irregular migration 'a trigger point for radical parties'
AfD's national leadership wants to govern

But what if that still does not lead to an AfD-led government? "Then we'll simply have to hold another election. That's just how it is," AfD parliamentary group leader Oliver Kirchner said on Compact TV.

That prospect, however, is unlikely to be welcomed by everyone within the party. "At the federal level, there is a strong interest in seeing the AfD lead the government in Saxony-Anhalt," observed political scientist Haußmann. Above all, the influential AfD co-leader Alice Weidel hopes to use an AfD-led state government as a stepping stone toward her long-term ambition of one day becoming Germany's chancellor.

DW also asked the AfD parliamentary group in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament, as well as a member of the party's state executive board, how the AfD is currently conducting coalition negotiations. Neither responded to our request for comment.

Despite its ongoing electoral success, the AfD continues to face considerable internal tensions between its fundamentalist and pragmatic factions. Even if the party were to enter government through a coalition, public skepticism toward it in Germany would remain substantial. Teresa Haußmann is among those who remain unconvinced: "Even if the AfD were to succeed in forming a coalition with another party, that fact alone would not make it a more democratic party."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: At least 15 killed in Pakistan mosque bombing near police station
articles.summary: A powerful bomb exploded Friday at a mosque near a building housing police offices in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 15 people and wounding 56 others, police and rescue officials said.

image.caption: In this photo taken with a smartphone, police officers secure a road leading to the site of a powerful bomb at a mosque in Kohat, Pakistan, on Friday. (B.S. Gillani/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A powerful bomb exploded Friday at a mosque near a building housing police offices in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 15 people and wounding 56 others, police and rescue officials said.
56 injured in attack in Kohat in northwestern part of country
A powerful bomb exploded on Friday at a mosque near a building housing police offices in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 15 people and wounding 56 others, police and rescue officials said.

The bombing occurred in Kohat, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province bordering Afghanistan, when an attacker apparently rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the mosque, said Zulfiqar Hameed, the provincial police chief.

Hospital officials have confirmed that five police officers and 10 civilians were among the dead, said Bilal Faizi, a senior rescue official. Most of those wounded were worshippers, he said. Some were in critical condition.
At least two armed gunmen also attempted to enter the police compound and exchanged fire with officers, police said.

Photos from the scene showed the outer wall of the police offices had collapsed and the mosque was badly damaged. Smoke rose over the site after the blast, which witnesses and residents said was heard far away, followed by gunfire.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack and expressed sorrow over the casualties. He directed authorities to accelerate rescue operations.
No immediate claim of responsibility
The attack came as violence has surged in the region, with security forces targeting militants.
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, but suspicion was likely to fall on the Pakistani Taliban, formally known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP.

The attack comes a day after a roadside bomb struck a security forces convoy in the northwestern Hangu district and killed six soldiers. Government troops also conducted raids in various areas on Thursday and killed 10 militants believed to be members of the Pakistani Taliban, the military and police said.

Pakistani Taliban have stepped up attacks on police and civilians in recent years. In 2023, a suicide bomber killed 101 people in an attack inside a mosque in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

The group is separate from but allied with Afghanistan's Taliban, which returned to power in 2021. Pakistan often accuses Kabul of sheltering the TTP and turning a blind eye to cross-border militant attacks. The government in Kabul has denied the allegations.

articles.title: Gadget guide: What students must know before buying
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Before spending their hard-earned savings on a new tool, student buyers need a reliable gadget guide to help them make informed and confident decisions on their next big…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Before spending their hard-earned savings on a new tool, student buyers need a reliable gadget guide to help them make informed and confident decisions on their next big purchase.
We’ve created a list of things that students should remember, know, and avoid before deciding on their next gadget purchase that will empower their studies in the coming years.
Where do I start planning?

From drafting research papers to delivering group presentations, a student’s daily routine requires a gadget that strikes the balance between performance, storage, build quality, and the right price. But with so many options on the market, knowing where to start your search can feel overwhelming.

The most common pitfall of student buyers is falling into extremes: They pay extra for high-end features that they seldom use, or they settle for cheaper and underpowered alternatives where they sacrifice the workflow needed to get the job done.

To avoid these mistakes, start by listing the specific software your courses or subjects do require. Identifying whether you primarily use productivity ecosystems or cloud suites like Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, or even heavy specialized software, is an essential first step in narrowing down your search for the next gadget purchase.
And here are some points to take care of when beginning to map out in searching for the next gadget:

items: Identifying your Primary Use Case — Everyone has a different set of needs, and that’s okay. Remember that computer science and multimedia students require a different set of technical specifications and hardware compared to those in education, humanities, or business courses that typically produce essays and presentations. Thus, it is important to determine what your current technology needs are. You might also want to ask yourself: “How will my next gadget benefit my studies in the long term?”
Mobility Check — Are you fine prioritizing raw power and screen space with desktops, or do you opt for portability in usage such as tablets, iPads, or laptops?

Check your current ecosystem — With the current technology that you have, check how it will be compatible with syncing with the new device that you’re planning to buy. In this state, are your existing devices compatible well with the devices you aim for–-like pairing an iPad with a Mac or MacBook? Or pairing an Android tablet with a Windows laptop?

Set a strict budget for the purchase — Allocate your financial resources wisely for your next device, and stick to what’s readily available to you. Don’t settle for less—and we recommend that if your needs require more powerful software for more powerful gear, then you would want to invest more financially.

blocks.text: RELATED STORY: New parental controls in iOS 27
The big four of gadget spending
When evaluating and canvassing for any gadget purchase, students usually look for these four major factors, ensuring they get the maximum value for their money before deciding on their next purchase:

items: Performance

For Laptops/Desktops: You need to focus on the processor (CPU) and memory (RAM). When using for general schoolwork, you might want to look for at least that is a mid-range processor (e.g., Intel Core i5, AMD Ryzen 5, or the Apple M-Series) that’s paired with at least 16GB of RAM for future-proofing. Enough RAM prevents your system from slowing down when you have multiple browser tabs open, a video call, and document editors open at once.

For Phones: You may want to opt for a phone with a mid-range to flagship processor. Aim also for at least 8GB of RAM, as well as a 90Hz or 120Hz display refresh rate that gives users reading long documents and scrolling through lecture slides smoothly.
Storage
For Laptops/Desktops: Always go for the Solid State Drive (SSD) over a Hard Disk Drive (HDD). Aim to go for 512GB of internal storage when you can.

For Phones: 128GB of storage is the absolute minimum in the current tech economy, where 256GB is the sweet spot for long-term usage, if you are looking to keep your phone for the next three to five years.
Price

For Laptops/Desktops: You might want to use student discounts outside the tagged price seen in physical stores. If you require software subscriptions or even accessories, you need to count that also towards the price. Standard entry-level laptops can currently range from ₱25,000 to ₱35,000, as the price of computer parts has gone up in recent months.

For Phones: Mid-range or flagship-killer phones can give more features that are close to the top-of-the-line features for half of their price. You might also want to check out back-to-school promos offered with software bundles so you can get more for less.
Quality & Upgradability:

For Laptops: Ask the retailers if the RAM and the storage are upgradable. This is crucial if you plan to expand the longevity of your laptops in the future. You might want to have a laptop that runs for 8-10 hours without needing to charge, especially if you have long days on campus.

For Phones: 5000mAh battery-powered phones are now typically more affordable in many phones. With this capacity, it already ensures that your phone can go on long days without the need to charge at a wall outlet. Your phone should also have developer support so that it can receive updates for at least 3-5 years. You will also want a durable phone that has scratch-resistant glass and that can withstand daily wear-and-tear and accidental spills.

blocks.text: What to look out for to avoid scams
Student buyers are a common target of scammers, and getting guides on how to safeguard your finances can help you get peace of mind.

items: Buy only through Authorized Sellers — Generally, we recommend visiting a physical store of your choice near you, so you can physically examine the gadget you wish to purchase. And should you have any questions, you can ask the sales representatives directly. However, if the store location is too far from your location, then you should buy from the official distributors or even from flagship stores of major online shopping platforms.

Be Extra Careful When Shopping in Local Marketplaces — When transacting through local marketplaces or online platforms such as Facebook Marketplace, always meet the seller in a secure, public place (like a busy mall or coffee shop) and test the device physically and ensure its full functionality before payment.

Check for Account Locks — If buying a second-hand device, check if the previous owner has wiped all personal data. If you see that the device is locked, it’s basically a bricked device and must be avoided.

blocks.text: Maximize online student discounts
Being a student means living on a tight budget, but your official academic email address is a golden ticket to substantial digital savings.
Before paying full retail price for the apps and media you rely on every day, students can use these discounts to ease the financial burden while boosting productivity and entertainment.

Spotify Premium and YouTube Premium offer a special discount for student subscriptions. Both streaming platforms offer ad-free, uninterrupted playback while doing your study sessions or an intense review for an upcoming quiz or examination.

For other software that is generally free or has cheap subscriptions, you may want to check with your school’s IT Office first about using cloud suites, as most schools provide free, full access by logging in with student credentials.

Additionally, productivity apps like Notion also offer free upgrades to their premium Personal/Plus tiers for users with .edu accounts, which unlock more features such as unlimited file uploads and advanced workspace organization.
Investing in a new gadget as a student isn’t about buying a flashy, top-tier device on the market; it is about finding the right tool for your academic journey.

Just like doing your research, your next gadget purchase should be as careful as you do your thesis: By doing extensive research and considering your needs, requirements, and proper resource allocation without falling victim to scams, you get value for your money’s worth.

articles.title: Poorest countries hit hardest by UK aid cuts under Keir Starmer government, new figures reveal
articles.summary:
Aid to lower-income countries fell by almost 7%, while higher-income countries saw their share of Britain’s aid budget increase

The world’s poorest countries were worst hit by British aid…

blocks.text: The world’s poorest countries were worst hit by British aid cuts under Keir Starmer’s government, while higher-income countries saw their share of aid increase, new figures reveal.
The latest figures released by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office show a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed countries and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.

The UK’s overall Official Development Assistance budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income (GNI), compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m. Further cuts are expected as part of the plans announced last year by Keir Starmer, who said money would be redirected towards defence spending.
Gideon Rabinowitz, the director of policy and advocacy at the charity network Bond, said it was “shocking” that the least-developed countries had borne the brunt of the cuts.

“The human cost of these cuts is already being felt, with critical humanitarian programmes – from maternal health provision in Sierra Leone to education for children with disabilities across Africa – already being forced to close,” said Rabinowitz.
“Marginalised communities around the world, including in climate-vulnerable and conflict-affected areas, are being left to pay the highest price for the Starmer government’s political choices.”
The highest share of aid, 18.4%, was spent within the UK on in-country costs for asylum seekers. This was a reduction from 20% in 2024.
The top three recipients of aid were Ukraine, Yemen and Afghanistan, but while aid to Ukraine is ringfenced, further upcoming cuts will see Yemen receive 28% less and Afghanistan 39% less by 2028/29.
While low-income countries saw their aid decline, it increased to lower-middle-income countries by 13% and by 2% to upper-middle-income countries.

Aid experts have warned that aid cuts by the UK, United States and Europe are forcing aid workers to cut anything but immediate life-saving support, even when this could lead to millions of avoidable deaths.
Earlier this month, a report by Active Learning Network for Accountability and Performance (Alnap) revealed that 64 million fewer people received aid last year as a result of the cuts.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Taliban security personnel stand guard women wait in a queue for food supplies donated during Ramadan, Kabul, March 2025. Photograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Across the humanitarian system, these cumulative reductions have contributed to the largest funding gap on record and forced increasingly difficult prioritisation,” said Jennifer Doherty, the report’s co-author.

“The longer-term consequences will depend not only on future decisions by donor governments, but also on how crisis-affected governments and other local and regional support systems adjust their own policies and approaches in response to reduced external assistance. Where those systems are unable to absorb the shock, there is a risk that more people will be left without support.”​
Bond, the charity network, is calling for the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, to reconsider the aid cuts introduced by his predecessor.

“What little remains of the UK aid budget must go where it is most needed: and contribute to the reduction of poverty and inequality – particularly in fragile and conflict-affected countries, where humanitarian needs are most acute,” said Rabinowitz.

articles.title: Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
articles.summary: Police reportedly fired into the air on Friday morning as they struggled to contain crowds jostling to secure a place at the tented site.

blocks.text: Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.
Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.
Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.
Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave.
The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.
During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.

More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.
The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror had no doubt she deliberately killed her children
articles.summary: It is the first time the juror, who refused to side with the others and acquit Clancy, has spoken publicly about his decision.

blocks.text: The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating.
Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated.
Warning: This article contains distressing details

The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window.

To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition.
The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder.
Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings.
"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday.
"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."
Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind.
"We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said.
The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster".

She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."

Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".
But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial.
The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations.
Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday.
In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began.
He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them".

During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis.
Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.
A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children.

However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association.

Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility.
The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.
Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial.
He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy.
He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset."
The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

blocks.text: Science·New

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia's cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
Leopardus tilcayo is a tiger cat identified as a new species through genetic testing
The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is ‌part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America.

It was found in Bolivia's lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 46 centimetres (18 inches) long and weighs around three pounds, making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, ​and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.

"Its fur is ​light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body," said Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.

Little is yet known about the cat's biology and ​lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be ⁠more active at night, Nogales Ascarrunz said.

Tiger ⁠cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, ‌said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart, of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Only 2 live individuals found so far
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said, "Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records."
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives ⁠in Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.

Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because "its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats," Nogales Ascarrunz said. "This made us wonder: What tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?"
The team analyzed DNA from 38 cats sampled across ‌several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
"We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal — subspecies or otherwise," Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.

"The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we ​estimate those lineages to have been physically separated," Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.

The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru's Yungas, naming it Leopardus ⁠tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca Empire that included the area it inhabits.
See some of the new species discovered in 2025
New species may be listed as endangered
The International Union for Conservation of Nature's red list, ⁠tracking the status of species, currently treats tiger cats as two "vulnerable" species with declining populations.

The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review ⁠will assess ⁠the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could potentially be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute ​in the Yungas, one of the region's most ⁠threatened ecosystems.

The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales Ascarrunz added.

"Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message," said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study.
"There are many undiscovered species out there ⁠in the world, and they are at risk of ‌disappearing before we even discover them."

articles.title: Manny Villar confident Ombudsman's graft claims over PrimeWater issue can be 'addressed'
articles.summary: Business tycoon Manny Villar, former Senate president and patriarch of the Villar Group of Companies, expressed confidence Friday that he and his family can dispute the graft charges leveled by the…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 7:40pm

Business tycoon Manny Villar, former Senate president and patriarch of the Villar Group of Companies, expressed confidence Friday that he and his family can dispute the graft charges leveled by the Office of the Ombudsman over the alleged poor service of their PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation.

Villar, the ninth richest Filipino according to Forbes' 2026 list, issued the statement shortly after the Ombudsman announced that two counts of graft have been filed against him, his wife former senator Cynthia Villar, their senator-children Mark and Camille, and brother Paolo over the PrimeWater issue.

"We have learned through media reports of the complaints reportedly filed before the Office of the Ombudsman. As of this time, we have yet to receive copies of the complaints and therefore cannot meaningfully comment on their specific allegations," he said.

"We are confident that, once given the opportunity to examine the allegations and the evidence supporting them, we will be able to fully and properly defend our rights and address the matters raised against us," the Villar patriarch said.
Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said the Ombudsman's investigation lasted about six months, covering PrimeWater's joint venture deals with various water districts from 2015 to 2022.
Officials of several water districts are also included as respondents in the complaint.
The Villar family members, Clavano said, were the beneficial owners of PrimeWater during the period of investigation.
In December 2025, the Villar Group sold PWIC to Lucio Co Group’s Crystal Bridges Holding Corp.
The former Senate president assured that they will handle the matter in adherence to the law.
"We respect the legal process and will respond to the complaints at the appropriate time and in the proper forum," he added.
He also advised against prejudging the issues without giving those concerned a fair shake.
"We ask that the legal process be allowed to take its course and that conclusions not be drawn before the parties have been afforded the opportunity to be heard," he added.

Clavano cited alleged violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act related to government officials and individuals giving undue injury or unwarranted benefits, and for entering into disadvantageous public contracts.

Senator Mark served as the secretary of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) from 2016 to 2021 before launching a successful senatorial bid in 2022. The Local Water Utilities Administration, which regulates the local water districts, is an attached agency of the DPWH.
Mark, his sister Camille, their parents Manny and Cynthia, all served as representative of Las Piñas City ahead of their tenures in the Senate. — VDV, GMA News

blocks.text: At least 16 people, including five police officers, have been killed after a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque in north-western Pakistan, according to a senior police official in Peshawar.
A gun battle is still ongoing between attackers and security forces at the mosque, near police headquarters, in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
One of the assailants has reportedly been killed, an officer says, and a rescue operation is under way.
In a statement, Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion."
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief inspector general Zulfikar Hameed described the attack as a "suicide attack" to Reuters news agency.
There has been no immediate claim of responsibility.
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif also condemned the blast.
Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, targeting the military and police.
Islamabad says the militants use safe haven in Afghanistan to train and plan attacks in Pakistan.
Afghanistan's Taliban government has denied the accusation and said militancy is Pakistan's domestic problem.

articles.title: DFA urges delay in implementing P1.5K passport fee until 2028
articles.summary: The printing agency responsible for producing Philippine passports is seeking a price increase, but Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Theresa Lazaro said the agency has been asked to…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 7:36pm

The printing agency responsible for producing Philippine passports is seeking a price increase, but Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Theresa Lazaro said the agency has been asked to defer the proposed hike until 2028.
Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito said that the APO Production Unit, Inc. has reached out to him with their concern.

“They are saying that if they fail to adjust the price, they might be forced to cease their operations and baka mamaya, wala tayong passport by next year… siyempre this will be a big problem,” Ejercito said, citing a letter from the APO Production Unit.

(They are saying that if they fail to adjust the price, they might be forced to cease their operations and maybe soon, we will not have a passport by next year… of course, this will be a big problem.)

Ejercito said that the printing agency is asking for passport prices to be raised from P950 to P1,500. However, there will be discounted rates of P1,200 for senior citizens and overseas Filipino workers.

“Ito pong sulat ng APO is a consequence of certain negotiations. Nung sinabi nila na gusto nilang iakyat ang halaga ng passport from the present P950 to P1,500, ang sabi namin sa kanila, kung puwede niyo i-postpone muna yung pag-increase,” Lazaro said in response.

(This letter from APO is a consequence of certain negotiations. When they said that they want to increase the price of the passport from the present P950 to P1,500, we told them that, if it is possible, to postpone the increase.)
Lazaro said that the request was reasonable, since the last increase was more than 10 years ago. Adding to this was the extension of the passport’s validity from five years to 10 years.
However, Lazaro said that they asked APO to defer this increase since there will be a next-generation passport, which will be launched in the middle of 2028.
“You cannot increase the price of a passport within three years,” Lazaro said, citing the Philippine Passport Act.

Lazaro said that if they increased prices by January as per APO’s request, it may affect the planned next-generation passport. She also said that the DFA would need to make a communications plan for a passport price hike.
Ejercito said that the DFA should let the Senate know if there is a need to subsidize the passports, but admitted that there was a tight fiscal space. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: What Trump’s attacks on mail-in voting mean for the midterms
articles.summary: The extraordinary danger is that a president who believes he is the law, and the law is him, remains intent on disrupting the electoral process

blocks.text: For the millions of Americans who vote by mail – almost a third of the country – the week began with significant uncertainty that they would be able to easily submit their ballot this fall, thanks to a March executive order from Donald Trump that aimed to restrict mail-in ballots. By Monday night, the supreme court restored a measure of order by rebuking the president and rejecting his plan – but Trump’s frothing response portends more danger for the rapidly approaching midterms.

Trump’s March order forbade the US Postal Service from delivering mailed ballots to anyone the administration deemed ineligible. The Department of Homeland Security, working with the Social Security Administration, would have devised that list of supposedly ineligible, noncitizen voters. On its face, the move appeared plainly illegal. One expert told the Guardian’s Sam Levine, “This is a wholly unconstitutional EO,” because ultimately the federal government cannot set election rules; only states can.

The plan was full of logistical problems, too. A whistleblower told Congress earlier this month that the Postal Service simply didn’t have the ability to implement the system safely, and that the whole plan was “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to Richard Blumenthal, the senator who handled the whistleblower complaint. State election officials also complained they would be unable to implement Trump’s restrictions this close to an election, even if they were deemed lawful. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin had already begun mailing out ballots before the supreme court ruled, and chaos would have reigned there and across the country had the court blessed Trump’s plan.

But it didn’t – and that sent Trump into a furor. In a lengthy post on Truth Social, in which he called mailed ballots “corrupt and out of control”, he singled out the conservative justices who had gone against him on that issue and this year’s ruling on tariffs. (Only the justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from the mailed ballot ruling; Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch, both nominated by Trump, did not.) “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” the president fulminated.

blocks.caption: Supporters of voting by mail rally outside the US Capitol in Washington DC on 15 September. Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA

blocks.text: His position is clear: the federal courts, the states that administer elections, the USPS – all of them should bow to his whims, regardless of what the constitution says. Trump has already shattered legal norms by appointing his former personal lawyer to head the Department of Justice and then continuing to treat him as a personal attorney. Just this week, in a remarkable scene at the White House, the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, served the role of White House press secretary, answering a wide range of questions from reporters on behalf of the president. A day later, a smiling Blanche attended a Trump rally for the GOP Senate candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, flashing an enthusiastic thumbs-up from the crowd.

The extraordinary danger of this moment is that a president who believes he is the law, and the law is him, remains intent on disrupting the electoral process. Trump’s claims about mail-in voting are false, as the Guardian’s George Chidi explained. The Brookings Institution has found: “An average total mail voting fraud percentage across the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 general elections of only 0.000043%, or about four cases of mail voting fraud out of every 10 million mail votes.” But Trump has been obsessed with the issue since 2020, when mailed ballots – which are typically counted last – evaporated his slim lead in some key states on election night. (Incidentally, Trump has voted by mail at least three times since then.) And more Democrats than Republicans vote by mail, so restricting mailed ballots also tilts the playing field towards the GOP.

State election officials are now working to assure voters that they can safely vote by mail this year, as Levine reported this week. But one can safely assume Trump will not stop pushing democracy to the brink.
Watch this race: Florida’s 27th congressional district

blocks.caption: A billboard featuring Florida politicians with roots in Cuba – Marco Rubio, María Elvira Salazar, Carlos Giménez and Mario Díaz-Balart – on 25 April 2025 in Medley, Florida. Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/AP

blocks.text: Trump won this Miami district by 15 points in 2024, when he aggressively promised a campaign of “mass deportations”. María Elvira Salazar, a Republican representative, easily held the seat, vanquishing her Democratic opponent by 20 points.

But Salazar is distancing herself from Trump this time around. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she says to the camera in a remarkable ad released on Thursday. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” She is facing a significant challenge this year from Eliott Rodriguez, a Democrat and former news anchor.
after newsletter promotion
Fact check

blocks.caption: Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally with Michael Whatley at the Gastonia municipal airport in North Carolina on 16 September. Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

blocks.text: During Trump’s speech address at a rally in North Carolina on Wednesday, which the Charlotte Observer described in an op-ed as a “dark, divisive” speech, he painted the Tar Heel state as a crime-ridden hellhole. “So nobody used to think of North Carolina as a dangerous state, criminally dangerous,” Trump said. “It was like North Carolina, it was beautiful, it was apple pie, right? And now it’s one of the most violent and one of the worst in the whole nation.” (An interesting pitch to voters: your state is the worst.)

But crime has fallen dramatically in North Carolina. Don’t take our word for it: only hours before Trump’s arrival in Gastonia, North Carolina, the White House blasted out a press release correctly noting: “In North Carolina, crime fell across all four major categories in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year, including a 12.4% drop in murders, an 18% drop in robberies and a 23% drop in motor vehicle thefts.”

items: George Zornick is the Guardian’s US political enterprise editor

Germany's government still undecided on fuel price relief

Germany's governing coalition is under pressure to show progress on bringing soaring gas prices under control ahead of two state elections this weekend in the northeastern states of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
On Friday morning, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's Social Democrat (SPD) state premier, Manuela Schwesig, told public broadcaster ZDF that Friedrich Merz should quickly implement a price cap.

The SPD is junior coalition partner with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative bloc (CDU/CSU) at federal level, but the parties have diverging ideas on how to address the soaring prices brought on the by the Iran war.
Despite Merz's insistence on Tuesday that gas price relief is coming quickly, the ruling coalition has yet to agree on an approach.
Germany weighs fuel relief as gasoline prices soar
Germany's conservatives have resisted the SPD's call for price caps and a windfall profit tax in favor of a fuel tax relief scheme.
Such a scheme was enacted in the first months of the Iran war and expired in June.
What the parties are saying about fuel prices in Germany

On Thursday evening, CDU General Secretary Franziska Hoppermann told a talk show that the coalition government was aiming for gas price relief of "around 22, 23, 25 cents per liter" by the beginning of October, without sharing concrete measures on how to reach that.
Germany's SPD Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has for months advocated a government-enforced price cap on gasoline and diesel, along with new taxes on heavy oil company profits.
"We are right now looking for solutions" said Klingbeil on Friday at a EU finance minister meeting in Dublin, Ireland.
"I want a clear, quick signal at the gas pumps right now," said Klingbeil, who is also vice chancellor. "I'm confident that we'll be able to get it done very quickly."
Klingbeil added he expects the European Commission to prepare proposals for a windfall profit tax by the next meeting of EU finance ministers in October.

Prices for gasoline and diesel have broke record highs several times over the past week. On Thursday, the ADAC motoring club reported diesel at a record-breaking €2.47 per liter ($10.72 per gallon) on average, and the lowest cost E-10 gasoline at over €2.30.

articles.title: India: Are food safety rules too much to swallow?
articles.summary: Recent raids at India's luxury hotels and a wider crackdown on its food companies have renewed the debate about food safety standards and their enforcement in the country.

image.caption: Consumers in India, the world's most populous nation, have long complained about poor hygiene at restaurants and cafesImage: Foto Prensa/Imago

blocks.text: Over the past few months, inspectors from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) raided kitchens at five-star hotels in New Delhi's Aerocity, including the JW Marriott and Andaz.

The inspectors reported "several serious food safety and hygiene deficiencies" at the Andaz, including "improper segregation of vegetarian and non-vegetarian food, pest activity, poor sanitation, inadequate food handler hygiene and improper storage practices."

During their visit to the JW Marriott property, inspectors observed "serious hygiene and sanitation deficiencies," including "unclean utensils and food-contact surfaces, visible particulate matter in the drinking water" and "inadequate pest control."
Both hotels said they were cooperating fully with regulators and reviewing or implementing corrective measures while reaffirming their commitment to food safety, hygiene and guest well-being.
Beyond hotel kitchens

The FSSAI crackdown is not limited to premium restaurants. The regulator has also issued more than 150 notices since July to leading food and beverage companies, primarily over misleading advertisements, health claims and labeling.
The concerns highlighted by the recent raids are reflected in the FSSAI's testing data.

In 2023-24 and 2024-25, authorities tested about 170,000 food samples each year, with roughly 1 in 5 found to be non-conforming. In 2025-26, the testing showed only a slight improvement: Out of 223,808 samples, 40,023 failed to meet safety or labeling standards, according to provisional data given to Parliament in July. "Non-conforming" includes adulterated, substandard, contaminated and misbranded food.
Urban kitchens driving demand for India's native spices
Sunil Ghadiok, a veteran hotelier with more than 45 years in the industry and founder of Enserve Hospitality and Management Services, said the "lapses" did not reflect the industry as a whole.

"Lapses occur because food safety depends on execution at the operational level. The bigger concern is not the existence of standards, but the commitment to overall hygiene and food safety," Ghadiok told DW. He said inspections needed to become more regular and go where the risk is.
"A complaint or a high-profile inspection should not be what brings food safety back into focus."
Rules versus reality
India seems to be struggling to routinely enforce its food rules.

FSSAI's Hygiene Rating Scheme for restaurants is voluntary. Businesses can apply for a rating, but they are not required to participate. Food-safety enforcement can therefore become highly visible when something goes wrong, while routine scrutiny is less apparent.

Yash Bhanage, founder and COO of Hunger Inc Hospitality, which runs The Bombay Canteen, O Pedro and Bombay Sweet Shop, said food safety issues were not necessarily linked to the size or reputation of an establishment.

"Food safety cannot be treated as a checklist that you complete because an inspector is coming. It has to become part of the operating culture of a restaurant," Bhanage told DW. The challenge, he said, was maintaining standards across changing staff, suppliers, multiple shifts and busy periods.
However, Bhanage said the current attention on food safety was "an opportunity for the industry to move from a culture of compliance to a culture of prevention."
The vital buzz securing our food and future
Manu Chandra, chef and restaurateur, said the industry's systems needed to reach further.

"A robust ecosystem has to be built around the [food and beverage] sector, which in many ways remains disorganized. There is a strong need for systems to be in place, and FSSAI's rules must trickle down, but right now they don't reach every corner of the industry," Chandra told DW. "Better traceability and stronger checks across the supply chain will help the sector in a big way."
The crackdown is already prompting some businesses to strengthen their own systems.
Samir Kuckreja of Tasanaya Hospitality, a Delhi-based hospitality consulting firm, said restaurants and hotels were seeking more help with food-safety audits, operating procedures and staff training.

"We first assess how the kitchen functions and tailor training to address specific shortcomings. Unannounced inspections followed by frequent audits usually offer better results than scheduled visits or self-assessment checklists," Kuckreja told DW.
India's food regulator also under scrutiny
The same question of enforcement extends beyond restaurants.
FSSAI's action against major food and beverage companies has included labeling and violations related to misleading claims.
Separately, the Supreme Court has been questioning the regulator over its proposed front-of-pack warning labels for packaged foods high in sugar, salt or fat.
The court has asked FSSAI to provide greater clarity on the scientific basis and thresholds for the proposed warnings, with the case due to return later this month.
The two issues are separate, but both raise a broader question about how effectively food safety rules are translated into practice.
The recent raids have shown what inspectors can uncover. The question now is whether that scrutiny becomes routine.
"The real measure of a mature food-safety system is what happens on the 364 days when nobody is inspecting you," said Bhanage.

blocks.caption: Rainfall during the monsoon season is currently 15% below averageImage: Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: India is expected to experience its weakest monsoon season since 2009, as a strengthening El Nino weather pattern curbs rainfall and raises concerns over crop yields and food inflation.

Cumulative rainfall during the June-to-September monsoon season is currently running 15% below the long-term average, according to the India Meteorological Department, local media reported. The initial forecast was just a 10% shortfall back in May.
If the deficit holds, this would be the weakest monsoon since 2009, when rainfall was 18% below normal.

A potential tropical cyclone could form in the Bay of Bengal in the final week of September, potentially easing the shortfall in eastern and northeastern India, Christian Werner of Global Weather Climate Analytics told Bloomberg.
He said the storm was unlikely to significantly shift the national picture, with the seasonal deficit expected to settle between 13% and 16%.

The lack of rain threatens both current harvests and the next planting cycle, adding pressure on food prices that have already risen for seven straight months, hitting 5.95% in August — the highest level this year, according to the Free Press Journal.
Rice, sugarcane and corn planting are running behind last year's pace, and the government has responded by permitting duty-free sugar imports and selling subsidized onions in some states.

articles.title: British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout
articles.summary:
Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police…

blocks.text: A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.

Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.

Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.

A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.
Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.

Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”
Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.
The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.

In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.

“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”

Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.
Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”
Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.
Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

articles.title: OpenAI ‘ethically hacked’ with help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot
articles.summary:
US cybersecurity researchers who conducted hack say ‘scope of what we could theoretically access was huge’

Cybersecurity researchers have hacked into OpenAI with the help of Anthropic’s…

blocks.text: Cybersecurity researchers have hacked into OpenAI with the help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot, in the latest example of security issues at the company.
A team at a US-based startup compromised a number of OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts, starting a process that enabled them to access their target’s software cache – and potentially more.
“The scope of what we could theoretically access was huge,” said researchers at Hacktron AI.

Initially, the research team used Claude, which can generate code for hackers, to access ChatGPT accounts via an OpenAI staff discussion forum hosted by the Discourse platform. They then made a harmless “pull request” – an attempt to change the code in a file – to OpenAI’s service on the GitHub software repository.

Hacktron reported the hack to OpenAI, having carried out the operation under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers for testing its systems. The researchers stressed that they had access to, but did not download, the code from the GitHub repository.
Despite initial use of Claude, the researchers said they were largely using OpenAI’s own cutting edge GPT-5.6 Sol model to carry out the hack, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings”, adding that the company had addressed the vulnerabilities that had been exploited.

Hacktron said AI tools had made a once-complex hacking task far easier and drastically shortened the time needed to plan and execute an attack. This is a common refrain from cybersecurity experts when discussing the impact of AI.

“Work that once required a well-resourced team and months of effort can now be compressed into days,” said Hacktron, which received a $6,500 payment from OpenAI under the company’s bug bounty programme.

The hack is the latest safety incident at OpenAI, which revealed in July that a “swarm” of agents – the term for AI tools capable of carrying out tasks autonomously – powered by its technology had hacked the AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test.

This week the San Francisco-based company revealed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” actions by its technology, and warned that the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”.

Anthropic made a fresh call at the weekend for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk. Anthropic also repeated warnings that unrestrained AI development posed an existential threat, concerns that some experts are sceptical about.
Donald Trump has rejected calls for a slowdown, citing a need to stay ahead of China’s AI industry and dismissing “negative forces … bringing up things that won’t happen”.

articles.title: Nigeria: Protests erupt over deaths of 37 miners in custody
articles.summary: Dozens of suspects accused of illegal mining were found dead in custody in Nigeria's north-central Niger State. Officials blame disease, while reports cite overcrowding and poor ventilation.

image.caption: Relatives of the deceased miners gathered in Minna after learning of the deathsImage: Ibrahim Ndamitso/REUTERS

blocks.text: Protests erupted in central Nigeria on Friday after 37 people believed to be illegal miners died while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps (NSCDC).
Police fired tear gas as dozens of demonstrators, including miners and their relatives, gathered in the central city of Minna, Niger State, armed with sticks and machetes, witnesses reported.
Niger State Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago told reporters on Thursday that the men had died in custody after being arrested earlier in the week on suspicion of illegal mining.

He called the incident "sad" and "tragic," adding that a committee of inquiry into the deaths had been established and was already working. The governor declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for the January elections.
The Nigerian government announced on Friday that the commandant of Niger state's civil defense corps had been suspended.
"It is an unfortunate incident, however, a full investigation will be conducted while the commandant under whose watch this happened remains suspended," the Minister of Interior said in a statement.
What do we know about the incident?
The suspected miners were detained in a series of arrests on Tuesday and Wednesday, said Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, head of the NSCDC in Niger, in a statement on Thursday.

Aniviye said that although the agency suspects the detainees died of disease, their bodies were sent to a local hospital for a medical examination to determine the cause of death. He did not specify the type of disease.
However, according to an intelligence report, "preliminary information suggests the fatalities may have resulted from overcrowding and inadequate ventilation within a detention facility."

A 40-second video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men, most of whom appeared to be teenagers. Volunteers wearing gloves stood over the bodies, while veiled women tried to identify their relatives.
Dirty gold: Nigeria's toxic water threat
Survivors describe a lack of ventilation

Dauda Shehu, one of the survivors, told the Associated Press that 65 detainees were packed into a poorly ventilated cell. "We were jampacked and there was no ventilation for us to breathe well," he said.

"All of a sudden, we realized that we could not breathe and we started scrambling to get fresh air," Shehu added. The detainees tried to get the guards' attention by banging on the cell door, he explained.
Spanning more than twice the area of Belgium, Niger State is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most of whom are lured by the hope of striking gold.

According to officials and experts, the scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger State is also fueling violence by criminal gangs known locally as bandits. These gangs tax miners and demand a cut of the extracted ore in exchange for access to the pits.

articles.title: For Aznar Shipping, going public means growth – and dodging third-gen curse
articles.summary: 'My main job is really to hand it over to the next gen,' the third-generation Aznar tells Rappler. 'Looking at the IPO process, the requirements, the standards that you are held to, it really…

blocks.text: 'My main job is really to hand it over to the next gen,' the third-generation Aznar tells Rappler. 'Looking at the IPO process, the requirements, the standards that you are held to, it really coincided with my interest.'

items: Kyle Alexander Aznar, the CEO of Aznar Shipping, is determined to break the generational curse that often affects family businesses by preparing to take the company public through an IPO.

The IPO aims to raise up to P737 million for fleet expansion and is part of Aznar's strategy to ensure the company's success for future generations, emphasizing professional governance and mentorship.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
As his family’s shipping legacy prepares to open itself up to the public, Kyle Alexander Aznar had an age-old curse on his mind.
“You know what they say, the third generation is the last generation,” the Aznar Shipping president and CEO told Rappler on Friday, September 18.

He was, of course, referring to the infamous adage that warns family fortunes rarely survives three generations. The first makes the money, second grows it, the third squanders what’s left. Gone, wasted, kaput.

The third-generation Aznar wasn’t about to let that happen. He was only 27 when he suddenly had to take over the family shipping business after his father died. Now 31 and at the helm, he sees one job as more important than simply making money.

“My main job is really to hand it over to the next gen,” Aznar told Rappler at the sidelines of his company’s H1 briefing. “We want our business to succeed — not just for my time. It’s really succeeding generations.”
His chosen way to keep the family ship afloat for another generation? Open it up to the public.

Aznar Shipping has filed for an initial public offering (IPO) that could see the Cebu-based company sell as many as one billion primary shares at an indicative price of up to P0.67 each, potentially raising P670 million in gross proceeds for the company. Another 100 million secondary shares could be sold through an overallotment option, bringing the total potential offer size to P737 million.

At this stage, everything still remains subject to book building and approval by the Securities and Exchange Commission and Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE). Aznar said the company is targeting a December listing, but stressed that he did not want to “jump the gun” on regulators.
Aznar is hardly the only old name sailing out of Cebu.

Cebu has long been one of the country’s biggest shipping hubs, producing generations of shipping families, from the Gothongs and Robles to the Cokaliongs and the Lims. The Aboitizes were once part of that club too, with Aboitiz Shipping eventually evolving into 2GO, now under the Sy family’s SM group. (READ: As Atlas Mining leaves by 2027, SMIC expects 2GO, renewables to fill gap)
But while many shipping businesses have remained private and closely held, Aznar sees public company governance as part of the antidote to the generational curse.

“Looking at the IPO process, the requirements, the standards that you are held to, it really coincided with my interest. That’s how I first started getting interested in it quite a few years ago,” he told Rappler.

The professionalization actually began before the IPO. Even before the company’s aspirations to go public, the shipping company already had independent directors sitting on its board. Aznar said he has been the only family member on the board for the past three years, surrounded instead by professionals whom he calls his mentors.
“I was just only 27 when I had to take over the company when my dad passed away,” he said. “I was humble enough to realize that I might not have all the answers, I might not always be right.”
That setup, he believes, has paid off.

blocks.caption: FINANCIALS. Aznar Shipping chief financial officer Dary Aran shares the company’s H1 2026 financial results. Photo by Lance Spencer Yu/Rappler.

blocks.text: Aznar Shipping’s revenue jumped from P59.2 million in 2023 to P223.9 million in 2025, when it booked P51.7 million in net income. In just the first six months of 2026, revenue reached P210.9 million while net income hit P53.2 million, already topping the previous full year.
The company currently operates nine vessels across four principal Visayas corridors, with cargo and rolling vehicles accounting for about 86% of first-half revenue.

The company wants to use IPO proceeds primarily for fleet expansion, with plans for newer vessels and, farther down the road, its own dry-docking facility. Aznar also said his company is not specifically hunting the customers of rivals.
“We’re not really eyeing specific players,” he told Rappler. “We’re following the market. We’re looking at complementary routes. We’re following our customers.”

blocks.caption: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday

blocks.text: If Aznar wants to test whether investors believe the family business can survive another generation, he’s choosing a challenging time to do it.

Even before getting to the stock market, the shipping industry is contending with elevated fuel prices. Aznar said fuel is the company’s biggest operating cost, although its move toward larger vessels has helped protect margins because capacity has increased much faster than operating expenses. (READ: DOE sees ‘no signs’ oil prices will fall as excise tax relief goes on table)

“Our new vessel could probably carry three or four times the load of our previous one. But the operating cost is more or less the same,” he said. “That’s how we’ve kept our rates affordable. That’s how we’ve protected our margins as well.”

So far, Aznar said demand has held up despite the broader economic uncertainty. “Our numbers are good,” he said. “The demand is there. The volume is there. And I believe it’s the right time to expand.”
But the bigger uncertainty may be whether investors will be equally ready.
The PSE index remains below the 6,000 level amid worries over slow economic growth and broader market uncertainty, well below the roughly 7,800 level where it ended 2019 before the pandemic.
Then there’s the very large elephant potentially barging into the stock exchange just weeks ahead of Aznar: GCash.

Mynt, the operator of GCash, is targeting an October 20 listing for an IPO worth as much as P92.3 billion, dwarfing Aznar’s planned offering. Would there still be enough liquidity left in the market after the biggest IPO in Philippine history when Aznar comes knocking in December?
The young shipowner, for his part, offered an appropriately maritime answer to the uncertainty.

“Market conditions, they’re out of our control. They’re just like the sea. You can’t always hope for calm waters,” he said. “What you can do is really learn to sail in rough conditions.” – Rappler.com
