Tamayo said the incident was an “isolated case,” and authorities have sent the students home to “control their emotions.”

“Sa ngayon, manatili lang tayong kalmado. Alam kong mabigat ito sa munisipyo ng Banga at sa mga magulang na nandito, pero wala tayong choice kung hindi pakalmahin muna natin ang ating mga sarili,” he said.
(For now, we must remain calm. I know this is a serious issue for the municipality of Banga and the parents here, but we have no choice but to calm ourselves for now.)

In a statement, the Department of Education (DepEd) said it was deeply concerned by the reported shooting incident, adding that its immediate priority was the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and school personnel.
It said it is ready to provide psychological first aid and mental health and psychosocial support.
“We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation,” the DepEd said.
In June, three students were killed after their two schoolmates opened fire at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City.
In August, two students died in the shooting incident at Ateneo de Zamboanga’s junior high school campus in Zamboanga City, including the alleged shooter himself.
This is a developing story, and will be updated. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Venezuela unblocks some news websites censored for years
articles.summary: Venezuela has restored access to 17 news sites that were blocked for years under Nicolas Maduro's administration. While activists welcomed the move, they noted that dozens more news portals, remain…

image.caption: Venezuela is starting to ease online censorship amid US-backed talks between the government and oppositionImage: Diko Betancourt/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Venezuela has lifted restrictions on several news websites that had been censored for years, its telecom regulator said.
Under the administration of Nicolas Maduro, who was captured by the US in January, hundreds of national and international websites, as well as various news portals, were censored.

Following Maduro's ouster, Washington has backed talks between the interim government, led by Delcy Rodriguez, and parts of the opposition. The decision to unblock the websites came ahead of the second round of talks in Caracas.
Dinorah Figuera, head of the opposition delegation in the talks, celebrated the decision in a post on X.

"Informing without fear cannot continue to be a privilege, but must be compliance with the law. This is a first step; there are still many media outlets missing, and they all have to return," she said.
Dozens of sites still blocked

VE Sin Filtro, a digital rights organization, confirmed that 17 news sites had been unblocked and that they were accessible through different internet providers. It added that 188 websites remain inaccessible, including 79 news portals.
Journalists and NGOs have long denounced the censorship imposed under Maduro.
Some users relied on VPNs to access these websites.
Deputy Communications Minister Gustavo Villapol said the decision was aimed at ending polarization.
"We can never again vilify people without having proof in hand; we cannot use communication for interests that are external to the vital meaning of our nation," he said on state television.
Maduro's fall stirs fears for Venezuelan, regional stability
Journalists respond with skepticism
Luis Ernesto Blanco, editorial director of Runrunes, one of the unblocked websites, said Thursday's move amounted to an official acknowledgment that public debate had been stifled.

Victor Amaya, who runs the TalCual news portal blocked in mid-2024, voiced skepticism that all censored sites would become accessible again, but said he hoped the change would lead to "a normalized communication environment."
The TalCual portal lost 60% of its audience due to the blockade, as well as much of its advertising revenue.

Media watchdog Reporters Without Borders last month said repression, censorship, restricted access to information and an increasingly hostile legal environment had severely stifled independent journalism in Venezuela.

articles.title: Germany's far-right AfD party copied Trump's playbook and won. It now hopes to use it to govern
articles.summary: From creating a deportation task force to revising history lessons in schools, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which won a resounding victory in the state of Saxony-Anhlat last…

image.caption: A supporter attends an election campaign event for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in a borough of Berlin in July. The Berlin state election is on Sunday and the AfD is polling in third place. (Sean Gallup/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Christian Machek is at a rally for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Berlin. Despite backing a nationalist party thousands of kilometres from the United States, he considers himself both an AfD and "Trump supporter."

The AfD secured a resounding victory in a recent regional election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the party is designated as right-wing extremist by the local domestic intelligence agency.
U.S. President Donald Trump celebrated the win on social media.

"I was happy [Trump] congratulated the AfD for a good campaign," said Machek, an Austrian Belgian citizen who lives in Berlin and says he works with the party in Germany’s parliament, the Bundestag, as an assistant to its spokesperson on religious affairs.
Ahead of Sunday's Berlin state election, the AfD party is polling just three points behind first place, according to a Sept. 10 survey conducted by German election research company Infratest-Dimap.

Machek, who also works for Europa Aeterna, which describes itself as a conservative political philosophy association rooted in Christianity, said the AfD is instilling a sense of patriotism and hope for the future. He sees Trump as a strong leader who also inspires national pride.
"I'm a Trump supporter from the beginning," said Machek. "It's a good sign. Just gives us hope that we're not alone."

The AfD fell just short of securing an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt, but it still has a chance of becoming the first far-right party to hold state power since the Second World War. In Germany, governments are usually run by a coalition of parties, meaning the AfD will need co-operation from other political parties or individual elected representatives to govern.

items: Far-right victory in German state expected to send shockwaves throughout the world
Germany's AFD could become 1st far-right party to hold state power since WWII. What could that mean?

blocks.text: AfD politicians cite Trump as the inspiration for some of their cultural policies, an area the party will control if it successfully forms government. They've even used the catchphrase "Make Saxony-Anhalt Great Again" on the campaign trail, an echo of Trump's MAGA slogan.
Although many AfD talking points pre-date Trump, the populist party is one of several around the world for which the U.S. president has provided a blueprint for how to gain mainstream support.

"Trump represents a model … of how you can whip up the base, how you can make electoral gains, and maybe even how you can seize power," said Eric Langenbacher, a political scientist with the American-German Institute in Washington, D.C.

"The fact that he's shown that what people thought were fantastical policies can actually be implemented, I think that is the biggest impact that he's had on the AfD, on Germany, and on many other countries as well."
AfD victory in Germany sparks protest, celebration
Hard line on immigration
Langenbacher said some of the AfD's strict immigration policies echo those implemented by the Trump administration.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD has said it wants to strip citizenship from immigrants who commit crimes, expand detention centres for deportees and create a "deportation task force," a term Trump started using during his 2016 presidential campaign.

"Sometimes, I feel like in Saxony-Anhalt, they just cut and paste from Project 2025," said Langenbacher, referring to the policy blueprint from the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think-tank, that has inspired some of Trump's efforts to reshape government and immigration enforcement.

The similarities between Trump and the AfD are evident to Anne-Christin Richter, 43, who lived and worked for a commercial vehicle manufacturer in Detroit for 10 years. She recently moved back to her hometown of Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt's capital.

Richter said her community feels more divided than when she left and though she can't attribute this directly to the AfD, she fears the party's anti-immigration rhetoric is fuelling racism in her community. Her daughters are both Black, and she says one of them was called a racial slur at a Magdeburg playground about a year ago. Richter said it happened when her daughter, now seven, tried standing up to an older child who was taunting immigrant children at the park.
A rise in racist rhetoric is something Richter said she also observed while living under Trump.
"You could see in the [Michigan] suburbs, suddenly, people started to say, ‘We don't want anybody to run around in our neighbourhood that's coloured,'" said Richter, whose boyfriend is Black.
"As soon as [Trump] was in power, everybody knew, ‘Now, we can say what we're really thinking,' right? And that's something I'm definitely afraid of."
AfD looks to revamp public buildings
If it successfully forms government in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD will control cultural and education policy, and it has said it will implement a widespread "patriotic shift" across society.

Hans-Thomas Tillschneider is an AfD politician in Saxony-Anhalt who wrote the sections on education and culture in the party's manifesto. He told CBC News at an AfD event in mid-August that he's inspired by Trump.
"We will make Germany great again," said Tillschneider. "We will rebuild our wealth, our freedom, our liberty. Rejoice, please. Don't be afraid."

The AfD's manifesto proposes following the example of a first-term Trump executive order to promote classical architecture in public buildings. It has specifically singled out for criticism the world-renowned Bauhaus movement and one of its original, 100-year-old buildings, which used to be an architecture school, in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD's manifesto calls Bauhaus untraditional and unnationalistic.

Barbara Steiner, the CEO of the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, said this kind of criticism predates Trump and has roots in the Nazi era, when the Bauhaus school was labelled "alien" and "lacking tradition." It closed under Nazi pressure in 1933 and reopened in Dessau in 1976 and is now a research, teaching and exhibition facility.
"It was wrong 100 years ago, and it is still wrong," Steiner said.

In its manifesto, the party also says it wants to revise history lessons in "all types of schools" to focus more on the country's achievements, arguing that emphasizing the negatives has caused Germans to harbour a "guilt complex" that damages national pride.

Trump has targeted cultural organizations using similar language. In March 2025, he signed an executive order claiming cultural organizations such as the Smithsonian Institution, which operates more than 20 museums, undermine U.S. achievements with negative ideologies.

"Rather than fostering unity and a deeper understanding of our shared past, the widespread effort to rewrite history deepens societal divides and fosters a sense of national shame," reads the executive order.

The AfD also promises to follow the U.S. in declaring Antifa, a decentralized anti-fascist movement, as a terrorist organization. It's something Trump signed into law as an executive order in September 2025.
Trump unpopular in Germany
Although numerous AfD supporters told CBC News they like Trump, polls suggest that the president is widely unpopular in Germany overall.

In March 2026, only 15 per cent of Germans considered the U.S. a reliable partner, according to Infratest-Dimap. That number climbed to 37 per cent among AfD supporters. Only one in eight Germans view Trump positively, according to a January 2026 survey from Infratest-Dimap.

Some AfD politicians may welcome praise from Trump as a boost to the party's visibility, said Thomas Greven, a political scientist at Berlin's Freie University, but supporting a foreign leader with an unpredictable agenda could backfire for the party.
"You don't want to be caught endorsing someone who is very obviously hurting your country's economy," said Greven.
Greven said AfD and MAGA are both inward-looking and ultra-nationalistic, making any long-term relationship tenuous, despite their perceived ideological closeness.
"The nationalism that unites them for this project will ultimately divide them and will divide nations."
Reporting for this story was funded in part by the Gordon Sinclair Roving Reporter Bursary.

articles.title: [OPINION] BARMM post-elections: Building a coalition that needs to govern
articles.summary: A healthy parliamentary democracy requires a credible opposition. The BFP should resist the temptation to create an oversized coalition simply to eliminate opposition.

blocks.text: After generally peaceful and democratic parliamentary elections, the region now faces a different — and perhaps more difficult — political challenge: how to govern after the votes have been counted.

Based on unofficial results, four political parties out of 13 appear poised to cross the 2.5% threshold for regional political party representation. The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) leads with 16 party seats, followed by the Moro Islamic Liberation Front-led United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) with 15, the clan alliance under the Bangsamoro Grand Coalition (BGC) with 8, and the Bangsamoro People’s Democratic (Raayat) Party with 1.

For the 32 district representatives, incumbent chief minister Abdulraof Macacua of BFP won in Maguindanao del Norte while MILF chairman Ebrahim Murad’s son, Mansor, won the seat in the Special Geographic Area. BFP won a total of 13 district seats, UBJP had 10, and the Adiong-led local party SIAP of Lanao del sur got six. Three other local parties got one seat each.

The six elected sectoral seats all went to the UBJP, thus affirming the sectoral and territorial dominance of the MILF’s UBJP. Two representatives from the indigenous peoples in BARMM were elected by them prior to September 14.

Overall, the 80-member parliament is now comprised of the following: a total of 30 seats for the BFP, 29 seats for UBJP, and 19 seats for the clan-led political parties. This parliament will govern for the next five years.

Many analysts would always equate the BARMM to the national government’s interests which is a given. The Bangsamoro Organic Law ties those interests due to national security risk management, natural resource management, devolution imperatives, and political economy. But that is another matter to discuss.

The numbers in votes tell only part of the story. No party has a majority. And that means the first elected Bangsamoro government will have to be built through coalition, negotiation, compromise, and trust. It also should not lead to a super majority coalition where there is no credible opposition.
What is needed is for a coalition to govern and not just forming a government. The former is difficult, the latter is easy.

With no party dominating the elections, the arithmetic is straightforward. The transition party incumbent BFP’s 30 party seats are not enough to govern alone. An alliance with the UBJP’s 29 seats would produce a dominant majority. But that would leave out the clan-led political parties which is critical for governance.
This is where the real politics begins.

The Bangsamoro parliamentary system was designed to encourage representation and negotiation. Unlike a presidential system where the executive derives a separate electoral mandate, a parliamentary government depends on the ability of political forces inside Parliament to construct a stable governing majority.

A government that survives by one or two votes on every major issue will be unstable. The new governing coalition should be dominant enough to survive disagreements, defections, political shocks, and difficult budget negotiations. The objective should be a stable parliamentary majority, not merely the minimum number needed to elect a chief minister.
Coalition governments inevitably require some distribution of executive responsibility.
But there is a danger. If Cabinet positions become rewards for delivering votes, the new government could reproduce the worst features of traditional Philippine politics.

The BFP-led coalition should instead adopt three principles: representation, competence, and accountability. Coalition partners should have meaningful representation in government. But ministers must also be competent to manage public institutions.

With the elections of the chief minister happening on the first day of convening parliament, a coalition government needs to be formed prior to that. In reality, the incumbent government under the BFP can initiate the formation. The goal should not merely be to find 41 votes to elect a chief minister. The goal should be to build a majority that can govern for five years.

But the first substantive agenda in coalition negotiations would be a governance agenda for a coalition government. The BFP could propose a Bangsamoro Governance Compact 2026–2031, signed by coalition partners before the election of the Chief Minister. The compact could establish a common agenda around on peace, development and governance.
This would shift coalition formation from “What position do I get?” to “What government are we going to build?” That distinction is crucial.
There is another delicate issue. The electoral transition should not be interpreted as the end of the MILF’s political relevance. The Bangsamoro Parliament itself is a product of the peace process.

The presence of former MILF leaders and representatives associated with the movement inside the elected political system is therefore not an anomaly. It is part of the transition from armed struggle to democratic politics.

blocks.caption: No single party gets majority of first-ever elected Bangsamoro Parliament

blocks.text: The challenge is to institutionalize that transition.

The most consequential negotiation may be between the BFP and UBJP. With 30 party seats between them, the two parties could form the nucleus of the next government. But the relationship would carry a significance beyond parliamentary arithmetic. The UBJP represents a political tradition deeply connected to the Bangsamoro peace process and the transition that produced the BARMM.

A BFP-UBJP coalition could therefore symbolize an important political transition: from the politics of the peace process to the politics of democratic parliamentary government, without abandoning the gains of the peace process itself.
The two should not be framed as competing sources of legitimacy. The Bangsamoro needs both.

The future government can draw legitimacy from the peace process, the ballot box, and the communities represented by elected district and sectoral leaders. The challenge is to bring these sources of legitimacy together. That would be a genuine measure of the success of the peace process.

The new parliament is likely to include representatives associated with powerful political families and local networks, including the Adiongs, Ampatuans, Gandamras, Hatamans, Mangundadatus, Midtimbangs, Sinsuat, etc.
These representatives should not automatically be dismissed as “clan politicians.”
They represent real constituencies. Their voters have concerns about roads, schools, hospitals, agriculture, fisheries, livelihood, security, local government, and access to public services.

The question is not whether these representatives have local political interests. Of course they do. The question is how those interests are incorporated into a transparent regional development agenda. The new government should establish transparent criteria for allocating public resources, while giving district representatives a legitimate role in setting regional priorities.

Representation must also mean geographic balance. The Bangsamoro is geographically and politically diverse. The composition of the executive should reflect this diversity. This is especially important for communities that historically have felt distant from the regional government like the Special Geographic Area carved out from the North Cotabato Province. A coalition government that promises inclusion but remains concentrated around the region’s established political centers will quickly lose credibility.
There is another important principle. Not everyone should be brought into the government.

A healthy parliamentary democracy requires a credible opposition. The BFP should resist the temptation to create an oversized coalition simply to eliminate opposition. This is what happened at the national level that should not be replicated.

An opposition can strengthen government. It can expose weaknesses, question expenditures, scrutinize appointments, challenge policies, and force ministers to explain their decisions. A Parliament in which everyone is part of the government risks becoming a Parliament where nobody is accountable.

The ideal arrangement is therefore: a broad governing coalition, a legitimate opposition, strong parliamentary committees, and active civil society. That is how parliamentary democracy becomes more than an institutional design. It becomes a political culture.

The 2026 parliamentary election should ultimately be judged not only by whether it was peaceful. It should also be judged by what happens after the election. The most important question of all: can the government be seen, felt, and deliver tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary Bangsamoro?. – Rappler.com

Tom Villarin is a political science professor at the Ateneo de Manila University. He served in the 17th Congress as Akbayan Party List representative. He also was former local government undersecretary under the Noynoy Aquino administration.

articles.title: Ottawa mayoral candidate charged for alleged death threats against Doug Ford and Mark Sutcliffe
articles.summary: A candidate for mayor of Ottawa is facing multiple charges for allegedly making death threats against Ontario Premier Doug Ford and incumbent Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe earlier this month.

image.caption: Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas was charged on Sept. 15 with two counts of criminal harassment and two counts of uttering death threats. (Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas/Facebook)

blocks.text: Ottawa
A candidate for mayor of Ottawa is facing multiple charges for allegedly making death threats against Ontario Premier Doug Ford and incumbent Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe earlier this month.
Charges filed in Kingston, Ont., against Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas cite social media posts this month
WARNING: This story contains descriptions of violent language and imagery.
A candidate for mayor of Ottawa is facing multiple charges for allegedly making death threats against Ontario Premier Doug Ford and incumbent Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe.

Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas was charged on Sept. 15 with two counts of criminal harassment, as well as two counts of uttering death threats allegedly made by social media posts between the dates of Sept. 6 and Sept. 13.
CBC News has obtained court documents that detail the charges and name the targets of the alleged offences as Ford and Sutcliffe, who is running for re-election as Ottawa mayor.
The documents say the conduct took place in Kingston, Ont., and could reasonably be expected to cause the premier and mayor to believe their safety was threatened.

Griplas has previously run for Ottawa city council in 2018 for Ward 1, which covers part of the eastern community of Orléans. He has had previous run-ins with the justice system that include multiple harassment charges.
He registered to run for Ottawa mayor on Aug. 21 of this year, the last day of nominations for the Oct. 26 election.

While the name posted on the public list of candidates is Geoff Nicholas, the candidate provided a full name including Griplas elsewhere on his nomination documents, which also include an address matching that on the charge sheet.
Social media posts
CBC News has viewed social media posts that remain on a Facebook page using the name Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas.

A post dated Sept. 6 shows a flyer for the Silver Lake campsite on fire with the words "kill Da Cliff" and another message partly obscured by the flames. It is captioned with the words "shame on you Mark!"
A video showing the same flyer was posted on Sept. 10, where the words "mayor must die" are fully visible.
A video post dated Sept. 12 shows a trashed room where the bedsheets have been streaked with a red substance, while other markings spell out the words "F-k Ford" and "Kill Ford."

In another video posted on Sept. 14, a day that is outside the period covered by the charges, a man with a concealed face can be seen brandishing what appears to be a revolver and screaming various phrases, including the words "dead, dead, dead."
The Kingston courthouse confirmed that Griplas appeared virtually on Thursday and remains in custody. His next court appearance is scheduled for Monday, Sept. 21 for a potential bail hearing.

Police were present at a campaign launch event Sutcliffe held on Wednesday. When asked if they are providing the mayor with a security detail, the Ottawa Police Service (OPS) declined to comment on any security measures or posture it is taking, citing the need to protect operational security and reduce risk to public safety.
But it said it is taking the threats seriously.
"In response to threats against Mayor Mark Sutcliffe, OPS assessed the information available and took appropriate steps to enhance our policing response," it said in a written statement.
Sutcliffe's office declined comment, while Ford's office said it won't comment on matters before the court.
The 2018 election
According to court documents from the Ottawa Courthouse, Griplas faced criminal harassment charges following the 2018 election.
In one case, that resulted in a guilty plea for mischief and a sentence of three years probation, while in two other cases he was found not criminally responsible.

Sutcliffe moderated a Rogers TV debate that Griplas participated in for his unsuccessful 2018 city council run. In his opening statement at that debate, Griplas said he had been previously incarcerated and was "brainwashed to perform an act of terrorism."

The bar to register to run for mayor of Ottawa is low. Candidates must pay $200 and provide signatures from 25 Ottawa residents, a rule that is common to all Ontario municipalities with 4,000 or more voters.
All of the signatures on Griplas's nomination documents are dated the day of or the day before he registered.
Starting on Sept. 1, mayoral candidates are able to access a voter list that includes the name and address of eligible voters across the city.

Candidates must submit a request. Elections Ottawa staff told CBC News that would produce a record and they confirmed that there is no such record of Griplas requesting those materials during the 2026 campaign period.

When CBC News asked city media relations whether they would be able to prevent him from doing so in the future, they said city clerk Caitlin Salter MacDonald, the top official responsible for the election, was not in a position to respond or comment further on that at this time.
Asked if Griplas will remain on the ballot on Oct. 26, Salter MacDonald said that certified candidates are required to be listed on the ballot in accordance with the Municipal Elections Act.

articles.title: Deepfake doctors peddling bogus cures are becoming more convincing — and very little can be done to stop them
articles.summary: Physicians warn AI-generated ads featuring the likenesses of prominent doctors are scamming patients out of their money, putting Canadians’ health at risk and eroding public trust. Yet there’s still…

image.caption: B.C. Provincial Health Officer Dr. Bonnie Henry, shown on a smartphone screen during a news conference in February 2021, is among the prominent Canadian physicians being "deepfaked" on social media. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, B.C. Provincial Health Officer Dr. Bonnie Henry became a familiar face across the country, appearing regularly at news conferences and in media clips.
Then her face and voice started popping up somewhere else: in AI-generated videos on social media, where her likeness was used to peddle supposed health products, including a prostate treatment.
"It really scared me initially, because it was so easy for people to make it look like I was saying things that were just not true," Henry recalled in a recent interview with CBC News.
Known as deepfakes, the online ads are "disturbing," she added, "because you know that people are taking things that are real and distorting them."

items: As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection

blocks.text: Henry is far from the only prominent Canadian physician whose likeness has been faked in questionable social media ads — and who has found little recourse.

Dr. François Marquis, chief of intensive care at Maisonneuve-Rosemont Hospital in Montreal, said he's heard from multiple patients and colleagues that videos featuring his likeness — all selling a range of pills or products — keep popping up on Facebook.

"This time I'm selling something that is supposed to fix your joints," he said, referring to the latest AI-generated ad. "And what is getting bolder is, now I'm offering $1 million if you're not a satisfied customer."
Canadian doctors selling meds online? Those are AI deepfakes

Marquis and other physicians say these videos are scamming patients out of their money, putting Canadians' health at risk, and eroding public trust. Yet there's still no clear method to get deepfake videos taken down, multiple doctors agreed.

items: He runs a secret AI slop empire from Vietnam. Here’s how we found him

blocks.text: "A few years ago, when this started to happen to me, nobody had any policies, nobody knew what to do," said Henry, who eventually filed cease and desist letters to multiple parties in hopes of combating the wave of deepfakes using her voice and face.
But she says her complaints are still hitting roadblocks today.

"I think our organizations — whether it's police services, whether it's universities, whether it's employment organizations — they're not really prepared yet to support people who are going through this," she said.
Don’t fall for this deepfake scam using AI-generated images of doctors, Quebec physicians warn
Scams 'only going to get more convincing'
The term "deepfakes" refers to a digital likeness of a real person, including their facial movements and voice, created by AI.
The videos have exploded online in recent years and the quality has dramatically improved, too, making fake videos of politicians, celebrities or physicians increasingly tough to spot.
One study found up to 50 per cent of people couldn't distinguish deepfakes from authentic videos about scientific subjects — and that was three years ago.

items: Will rogue AI development mean the end of humanity? Experts weigh in
AI 'fearmongering' could harm Canada’s rare opportunity, says top CEO

blocks.text: "It's only going to get more sophisticated," warned Timothy Caulfield, a researcher and professor focusing on health law and science policy at the University of Alberta.
"These kinds of scams — and that's really what they are — are only going to get more convincing."

While there's no major Canadian research yet on the prevalence of doctor deepfakes on platforms like Facebook and TikTok, a 2024 report in the British Medical Journal noted they're increasingly common in the U.K., while American policymakers are considering a bill — dubbed the "NO FAKES Act" — to combat the growing trend of AI deepfakes in the U.S.
Canadian physicians say more research and recourse is needed here as well, alongside public education to help patients avoid getting scammed.
New AI deepfakes law 'too little, too late' for Halifax woman
Concern over fake drugs, dangerous health advice
Marquis recalled a victim of one deepfake scam who came looking for him in the ICU, wanting his money back for pills that were never delivered.
"It was very sad, because that person invested hundreds of dollars in those pills and never received anything," he said.

items: Why are AI leaders calling for a slowdown?
Why are there suddenly so many data centres planned in Canada? Your questions answered

blocks.text: Marquis's bigger fear is patients ordering and consuming fake drugs, or following false advice to stop their medications.

Despite those risks, he routinely struggles to get deepfake videos taken down before new ones pop back up — even though he's flagged them to social media platforms, Quebec's medical college and the police.
"Basically I was told that there's nothing they can really do," he said.
He lost $3,000 after falling for a fake Carney ad pushing for crypto
Canada lacks 'co-ordinated response'

As part of an effort to clamp down on deepfakes and other AI-related security issues, the federal government has in recent years taken measures such as expanding the Canadian AI Safety Institute and introducing legislation to combat non-consensual sexualized deepfakes — dubbed the Protecting Victims Act — and AI-generated electoral misinformation.
Anyone who may have been a victim of cybercrime can file a police report or contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, a federal bulletin from 2024 noted.
CBC News has contacted Science and Economic Development Canada for comment on how it is tackling medical deepfakes, specifically.

items: Canada's AI strategy aims to make health data more accessible. How will it protect privacy?

blocks.text: Dr. Fahad Razak, an internist at St. Michael's Hospital and Canada Research Chair in Healthcare Data and Analytics at the University of Toronto, said there still isn't a "co-ordinated" response to the problem across Canada.

"And what makes it very challenging is that a lot of the media we consume in Canada is not generated in Canada," he added. "We don't have enforcement mechanisms and the ability to save and filter out content from certain parts of the world."
Fact check: Ads on Facebook link to Carney deepfakes
Videos selling products can be 'red flag'
For now, much of the onus to spot and avoid deepfake scams falls on the public.
"I think that any time content is being pushed to you and they're selling a product, that should be a major red flag," said Caulfield.

That's even more true for Canadian doctors supposedly selling health drugs or treatments, since provincial and territorial medical colleges enforce strict standards, noted the Canadian Medical Association (CMA) in an awareness post earlier this year.

items: Quebec physicians warn of deepfake scams using their likeness to sell medications

blocks.text: "Although the precise rules vary, the intent is clear: doctors cannot publicly endorse health products in ads, on social media or in interviews," the CMA stated. Those products are defined by Canada's Food and Drugs Act as any regulated drugs, biologics, medical devices or natural health products.
Razak encouraged people to be highly skeptical of any videos featuring a doctor selling medical goods.
"If you think about your own physician experience, how often is a physician pulling out a drawer of material and trying to sell you something?" he said.
"That's not how our health-care system works."

articles.title: ‘Intentional ramming’: China Coast Guard damages Philippine ship in West PH Sea
articles.summary: The BRP Datu Magat Salamat is en route back to Coron to assess its seaworthiness

blocks.text: RAMMING. The PCG releases footage of the CCG ship harassing and eventually, ramming, a BFAR vessel.
Philippine Coast Guard
The BRP Datu Magat Salamat is en route back to Coron to assess its seaworthiness

items: A Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessel, BRP Datu Magat Salamat, was damaged after being intentionally rammed by a China Coast Guard ship while en route to deliver fuel to Filipino fisherfolk.
The Philippine Coast Guard reported no injuries among the crew, which consists of personnel from both the PCG and BFAR, and the vessel is returning to Coron to assess its sea-worthiness.

The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea condemned China's actions as reckless and in violation of international maritime laws, urging China to cease dangerous activities that threaten lives at sea.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines — A Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessel sustained damage to its main railings, metal stanchions and supports, as well as deck fixtures and equipment, after a China Coast Guard (CCG) ship rammed it on Friday, September 18, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said.

In an online briefing with reporters, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said it was a case of “intentional ramming” by the CCG vessel. A day earlier, the Philippine vessel ran aground at Hasa-Hasa (Half Moon) Shoal.
The BRP Datu Magat Salamat has since decided to cut short its mission and was en route back to Coron to assess if it was still sea-worthy, said Tarriela.

blocks.caption: ‘Intentional ramming’: China Coast Guard damages Philippine ship in West PH Sea

blocks.text: The BRP Datu Magat Salamat was supposed to bring fuel to Filipino fisherfolk in Abad Santos (Bombay) Shoal when the CCG ship (CCG-21585) used dangerous manuevers on the smaller BFAR ship — cutting across her stern before “striking” or ramming the slightly smaller BFAR vessel.
No injuries were reported from the BRP Datu Magat Salamat, which is manned by a mix of PCG and BFAR personnel.

Tarriela said the 21-series CCG ships are the smallest in the fleet, at under 50 meters long, and are the most agile. In the past, Tarriela said, vessels in this class have been involved in incidents of harassment in the West Philippine Sea, including during resupply missions to Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal, a Philippine Navy outpost in the West Philippine Sea.
Abad Santos Shoal is just around 54 nautical miles away from Palawan and is within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone (EEZ) in an area Manila calls the West Philippine Sea.

In a statement, the National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea condemned China for a “reckless act” that breached the 1972 Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs), the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and the 2016 Arbitral Award.

“The NTF-WPS calls on China to cease dangerous and unlawful actions that endanger lives at sea. We will continue to exercise our rights under international law with restraint, professionalism, and firm commitment to the security and dignity of the Filipino people,” said the inter-agency NTF-WPS.

China claims almost all of the South China Sea to include the Philippines’ EEZ. China has also refused to accept the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award, which affirmed the Philippines’ 200 nautical mile EEZ and deemed China’s sweeping “historical” claim invalid. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Transportation chief Lopez appeals to Senate to fund EDSA busway in 2027
articles.summary: The Department of Budget and Management’s proposed 2027 budget does not include funding for the EDSA Busway

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Transportation Secretary Banoy Lopez appealed to the Senate finance committee to restore funding for the EDSA busway in the 2027 national budget.
The Department of Budget and Management’s (DBM) proposed 2027 budget does not include funding for the EDSA busway, also known as the National Capital Region Busway project.
Lopez said the Department of Transportation (DOTr) had requested P1.756 billion for the project, but no allocation was included in the proposed budget.
“The one that will suffer are the commuters who are using the busway carousel,” Lopez said during the Senate finance committee budget hearing on Friday, September 18.
The EDSA busway serves around 63 million passengers annually, Lopez said.

Without funding in 2027, Lopez raised concerns about the DOTr’s ability to continue improving the busway, including planned stations and measures to keep them accessible to senior citizens and persons with disabilities through elevators.
Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito expressed support for Lopez’s appeal and the continued improvement of the EDSA busway.
Three busway stations are targeted for completion this year, with three more planned for completion in 2027.
The Management Association of the Philippines (MAP) also backed Lopez’s call for funding for the EDSA busway.

“All measures must be given to ensure the primacy of the government’s policy of mass transit over private vehicle use on our limited road space. To do less would only add to the massive traffic problem,” MAP said in a statement on Friday.
The Move As One Coalition first flagged in August the absence of funding for the EDSA busway and other key public transportation programs in the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program.

“A supermajority — 94% — of Filipinos do not own cars; 94% support the construction of safer, wider bicycle lanes and walkways. Why are their mobility needs not reflected in the proposed National Expenditure Program 2027?” the coalition said in a statement.
Aside from the EDSA carousel, several train projects and fuel subsidies were also left unfunded in the 2027 budget proposal.

articles.title: Labor’s plans for visa overstayer detention centres branded a ‘Donald Trump twist’ on immigration
articles.summary:
Australian Greens senator compares government’s policy to ICE as Tony Burke calls it a ‘ridiculous claim’

  • Get our
articles.byline: Caitlin Cassidy and Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: The federal government’s move to reopen detention centres for visa overstayers, overseen by compliance officers, has drawn comparison from the Greens and advocates to Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown in the United States.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, was careful to downplay any similarities when he announced the federal government’s immigration plan on Thursday, which includes reducing the roughly 77,000 unlawful non-citizens in Australia.

He told the National Press Club the policy was returning to a “routine process” that existed prior to 2015, whereby overstayers were brought into detention centres if their visas lapsed prior to securing flights home.
“This is not the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries,” Burke said.

Burke said 100 new compliance officers would be hired to round up overstayers, and an additional 250 beds would be freed, as well as potentially repurposing a 100-bed quarantine facility in Victoria. He said most people would be placed in detention for a matter of weeks, and encouraged to leave of their own accord.
Greens immigration spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said Labor should make visa processes and appeals faster rather than focusing on net migration figures.
“This is where Labor has sunk to, reheating Tony Abbott’s immigration attacks, with a 2026 Donald Trump twist,” he said.
“Labor’s new immigration jails will be run by the same exploitative US private prison multinational that is already abusing people’s rights in immigration detention here.
“If the Minister doesn’t want these policies to be compared to ICE, he should not behave like ICE.”

In 2025, the US private prison company Management and Training Corporation won a $2.3bn contract to run onshore detention in Australia under its local subsidiary Secure Journeys, despite serious concerns about MTC’s track record. MTC is one of a handful of private prison operators running ICE detention facilities.
Burke told Guardian Australia Shoebridge was making a “ridiculous claim” by comparing Labor’s policy to the Trump administration’s immigration stance.

“The Green Party knows it isn’t true,” he said. “We are simply going back to what Australia had done for decades until mandatory cancellation started, which was to have around 250 beds used when someone no longer had a visa but was refusing to leave.”

The shift occurred under then-immigration minister, Peter Dutton, who introduced mandatory visa cancellations for criminal offenders in 2014, which rapidly filled detention centres and saw the department quietly pivot to issuing short-term bridging visas for low-risk overstayers to manage voluntary departures.
Ramping up removals forms part of Labor’s plan to bring net overseas migration down from 292,100 to meet budget forecasts of 245,000 in 2026/27 and 225,000 each year thereafter.

The former head of the Australian Human Rights Commission, Dr Gillian Triggs, told AAP that Australia’s pre-2015 migration detention regime put children in a “horrific pipeline”, with hundreds held in detention without education, most of whom were “severely mentally and physically ill”.
In 2023, a landmark high court decision outlawed indefinite detention without reasonable prospect of being returned to one’s own country, but it’s unclear how that might apply to this change.

The CEO of the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre, Kon Karapanagiotidis, said the federal government had demonstrated “the right to seek asylum and the right to work while seeking safety remain in danger”.
after newsletter promotion

“Minister Burke went to great lengths to reassure Australians this would not look like Donald Trump’s immigration raids,” he said. “But look at what is actually being planned … This will double Australia’s immigration detention regime.
“We will not stand by while migrants and refugees are used as political punching bags.”

Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the immigration department, downplayed the ICE comparisons, pointing out that up until 2015, compliance officers wore “shirts and a tie”, not military gear and were unarmed.
“They operated completely differently,” he said. “They did not enter any premises of any employer without the permission of the employer or a warrant.”
Rizvi said one of the “biggest functions” of the compliance team was educating employers about how to check the working rights of foreign employees, which he said “all appears to have stopped”.

“Given that this cohort is at record levels and grows by around 1,000 per month, what should the government do about a cohort with no remaining right to be in Australia, noting that this cohort will be highly vulnerable to exploitation and live in the shadows of society?” he said.

The legal director at the Human Rights Law Centre, Sanmati Verma, said the federal government should invest in protection for undocumented migrants who had been exploited at work rather than “needlessly expanding the punitive immigration detention network”.
“Rounding up undocumented migrants and locking them in detention is a profoundly anti-worker proposal that undermines the Albanese Government’s commitment to stamping out modern slavery,” she said.
With Australian Associated Press

articles.title: Retail sales bounce back in Great Britain amid brighter signs for economy
articles.summary: Latest data to defy economic gloom shows 0.5% rise boosted by purchases of sports items, aircon units and fans amid heatwaves

blocks.text: Retail sales across Great Britain unexpectedly rose last month, the latest economic indicator to defy gloomy forecasts as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to present next month’s budget.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold rose 0.5% month on month in August, defying analyst expectations of a 0.2% fall.
It marks a significant bounce back in consumer spending after a 0.5% month-on-month fall in July.
The summer heatwaves fuelled increased sales of items including fans, air-conditioning units, sports merchandise and clothing in the three months to August.

The unexpected sales boost is the latest positive update on the state of the economy for the government, after a surprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic product in July that was reported by the ONS last week.

“August’s warm weather delayed the usual shift towards autumn purchases, but retailers successfully kept consumers spending,” said Sandra Prince, the head of consumer at Lloyds. “The late bank holiday weekend and back-to-school shopping are also likely to have supported demand, with online sales among the areas seeing the biggest boost.”
Across the three-month summer period sales rose 2.4% year on year, again significantly above forecasts of a 1.9% rise.

Among the strongest performers were department stores, which recorded a sales rise of 1.8% month on month in August – a bounce back after a fall in July, which the ONS attributed to stock availability problems.
Non-store retailing, primarily online shopping, rose by 1.7% month on month, fuelling a strong summer where there was a 5.4% sales rise across the three-month period.
Retailers selling alcohol and beverages performed well across all three months to August 2026, the ONS reported, which they attributed to promotions, the hot weather and the men’s football World Cup.

Fuel sales dropped again, down by 1.7% in August and 2.5% across the three-month period, as motorists cut back on non-essential journeys after big increases in the price of petrol and diesel since the start of the Iran war in February.
after newsletter promotion
UK petrol prices have hit the highest level in four years as the conflict in the Middle East intensifies.

On Thursday the Bank of England monetary policy committee voted to hold the base rate at 3.75%. However, it indicated that the latest rise in energy prices because of the conflict is likely to result in a rates increase to keep inflation in check. Inflation rose to 3.1% in August, from 2.9% in July.
“There are some challenging headwinds for consumers to navigate as we head into autumn,” said Andy Carlisle, the consumer goods and retail lead at Accenture.

“Higher energy bills, food, fuel and transport prices continue to weigh on purse strings. We’re beginning to see consumers preparing for these pressures, prioritising everyday needs while showing greater caution around discretionary and bigger-ticket purchases.”

articles.title: Malaysia: Jailed ex-leader Najib allowed house arrest
articles.summary: Convicted in the 1MDB scandal for embezzling millions, former Prime Minister Najib Razak had repeatedly sought clemency. Malaysia's king has now granted him a "conditional pardon."

image.caption: Najib Razak has denied wrongdoing and repeatedly appealed his conviction Image: Hasnoor Hussain/REUTERS

blocks.text: Malaysia's graft-convicted former Prime Minister Najib Razak was granted royal clemency and will be allowed to sit out the remainder of a six-year jail term in house arrest, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's legal department said on Friday.
King Sultan Ibrahim "has granted a conditional pardon" to Najib, "allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest" until August 23, 2028," lawyers said.
The conditional pardon is subject to the payment of 50 million Malaysian ringgit ($12.3 million; €10.7 million).
Billions stolen from state funds

Najib, 73, is currently serving a six-year term in prison for his role in the 1MDB corruption scandal, named after 1Malaysia Development Berhad, a state investment fund he co-founded while serving as prime minister from 2009 to 2018.

In 2020, Najib was originally sentenced to 12 years in prison for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving $10.3 million funneled into his bank accounts. He began his sentence in 2022.

In a separate case, Najib was convicted in December 2025 of abuse of power and money laundering, accused of misappropriating nearly $569 million from 1MDB. He was fined $2.8 billion and sentenced to another 15 years in prison, which is to take effect after his existing sentence ends. He is currently appealing that conviction.
Malaysia's former PM guilty in major corruption scandal
It was not specified on Friday whether the clemency applied to the first conviction affects the second case.
Royal clemency and the law

It is not the first time Najib has received a pardon. Under the previous king in 2024, Najib saw the sentence from his first conviction of 12 years cut in half, and fines reduced. At the time, he had sought unsuccessfully to secure house arrest.
Najib's ⁠legal ​team has not yet commented on Friday's decision, and it is not immediately clear when the former leader will be released into house arrest.

Investigators allege the 1MDB scandal involved at least $4.5 billion in state funds that were stolen and laundered by top executives and associates of Najib. Najib has always denied wrongdoing and has tried to frame himself as a scapegoat.

blocks.caption: Najib still enjoys political support in MalaysiaImage: Hasnoor Hussain/REUTERS

blocks.text: The embezzlement scandal sparked national outrage in Malaysia and led to the 2018 election defeat of Najib's party United Malays National Organization (UNMO), which had governed the country since independence from Britain in 1957.

The scion of a prominent political family, Najib was long seen as untouchable. He still holds political clout in Malaysia, and Friday's royal clemency could lead to questions over equal treatment under the law.

articles.title: Japan raises interest rate to new 31-year high to curb rising prices
articles.summary: Central banks around the world have hiked rates as high energy prices are pushing up inflation.

blocks.text: Japan's central bank has raised its main interest rate to a fresh 31-year high as it continues to move away from decades of ultra-low borrowing costs and as the country faces increasing economic pressures.
In a widely expected move on Friday, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) increased the rate from 1% to 1.25% - a level not seen since 1995.
It comes as major central banks around the world are hiking rates as higher energy prices caused by the Iran war are helping to push up inflation.
On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in over three years, while the European Central Bank also increased its borrowing costs earlier this month.
The BOJ has been raising the rate since 2024, when it stood at minus 0.1%. It has now hiked rates six times in the last two and a half years.
Since then the bank has been steadily putting up the rate as it tries to reach a level similar to other major economies.
When a central bank raises rates, known as tightening monetary policy, the country's currency usually becomes stronger as it makes the it more attractive to traders.
"One of the world's last sources of ultra-cheap money is disappearing," said market analyst Lale Akoner from investment company eToro.
Japan is facing several economic challenges including a persistently weak yen, rising prices and a shrinking workforce.
Official figures published on Friday ahead of the BOJ announcement showed that inflation eased slightly last month.
Core inflation fell to 1.7% in August from 1.8% the previous month but remains close to the bank's 2% target level.
While Japan's inflation rate is not high by international standards, rising prices are a relatively new development in the economy.
Until recently the country had experienced very low inflation or deflation - falling prices - for around three decades.
Global oil and gas prices have risen this year as the Iran war caused major disruptions to shipments through the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route.
Japan is particularly vulnerable to those supply interruptions as it is heavily reliant on energy from the Middle East.
The country's currency has also been under pressure in recent months.
In August, Tokyo and Washington confirmed that they had jointly intervened to halt a slide in the yen after it fell to a fresh 40-year low.
The coordinated intervention was the first since 2011, when both countries took action together to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake and tsunami that hit eastern Japan.
Both Japan's Ministry of Finance and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time that they would not hesitate to conduct more joint interventions in the future.
Bessent has also been ramping up pressure on the BOJ to raise interest rates to help support the yen, calling on its Governor Kazuo Ueda to "do the right thing".
"If [the yen] remains weak despite higher rates, the resulting inflation pressure could force the BOJ to tighten faster than markets or Japan's government would like," Akoner said.

articles.title: Japan raises interest rates to 31-year high to curb impact of rising prices
articles.summary: Increase from 1% to 1.25% follows US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank tightening monetary policy

blocks.text: Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat high global inflation linked to the war in Iran.
The Bank of Japan voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995.

The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank of England on Thursday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75% but warned they could soon rise amid the fallout from the Iran war.

The BoJ has been raising rates since 2024, when it lifted its base rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year, to levels that prompted policymakers to intervene to stabilise the currency. The Japanese currency weakened about 0.7% against the dollar on Friday.
The vote to raise rates was not unanimous – with two board members dissenting to the increase.

“The tone of the statement, along with two dissenters for the decision to raise rates, leaves lingering doubts that Japan’s central bank will be cautious in tightening monetary policy further,” ⁠Fred Neumann, the chief Asia economist at HSBC, said.
“While back-to-back hikes appear unlikely, investors will look for clues as to whether officials are prepared to raise interest rates again in December.”

The drop in ​the yen helped the Nikkei stock market index to rise nearly 2%, while the Japanese two-year government ‌bond yields, which are most sensitive to ‌monetary policy expectations, fell four basis points to 1.82%.
European stock futures slipped 0.35%, indicating a lower open.
after newsletter promotion

Prashant Newnaha, a senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said the BOJ reiterated its concerns that underlying inflation could deviate upwards from its 2% target, but “we don’t see a smoking gun supporting a back-to-back hike ‌in October”.
He said: “We stick with our call for rate hikes roughly every quarter with the next 25 basis points hike in December.”

Hopes of ​alternative ways for oil supply from the Middle East to ​reach markets pushed Brent crude futures down as much as 1.5% to $103.29 a barrel even as concerns about strikes between Saudi Arabia and ​Yemen’s Houthis lingered.

articles.title: VAR's mission creep a problem for football
articles.summary: After a decade of use, questions around VAR in football are louder than ever. Has the technology strayed too far from its remit?

image.caption: How much technology is too much? VAR appears to have strayed too far from its original missionImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another domestic football season is underway and already, in mid-September, the shortcomings of technology in sport are at the center of the discourse once again.

The video assistant referee (VAR) is perhaps the most discussed technology in modern sport. While video replays have been in use for years in sports like American football, rugby or cricket, it has only been a decade since the International Football Association Board (IFAB), the highest regulatory authority in the sport, approved the use of VAR.

With artificial intelligence (AI) reportedly reaching dangerous levels of development and technological optimization of people's lives at an all-time high, it is perhaps a pertinent time to consider the use of technology in sport. Has it finally evolved from a supporting role to an all-powerful, game-altering one?

"The idea behind VAR was that technology could reduce human error while leaving the referee in charge," Susmit Gulavani, an assistant professor in AI and machine learning in sport at the University of South Carolina, told DW.

"Over time, however, VAR has expanded in both its use and its influence. The introduction of newer technologies, such as AI-assisted Semi-Automated Offside Technology (SAOT), has made it an increasingly central part of decision making. While these advances have improved the precision of offside decisions, they have also raised expectations that technology should deliver perfect outcomes," he said.

"That is where the sense of "mission creep" comes from. VAR is now expected to resolve almost every contentious decision, even though many incidents, such as fouls or handball decisions, still require human interpretation."

That pursuit of perfection often leaves fans waiting and confused, and it breaks up a game that is fast and fluid. The World Cup this summer was evidence of that. And yet, if anything, the technology looks like it is finding more ways to embed itself into the sport.
VAR in the Bundesliga under the spotlight
It has been nine years since VAR was introduced to the Bundesliga.

After the World Cup, German officials confirmed that VAR will also be allowed to have a say in second yellow cards and corner kicks in the Bundesliga. Granting technology additional powers did not go down well with organized fan groups in the country though, who launched a coordinated campaign calling for VAR to be scrapped in August this year. The broad message was that the technology has "robbed football of its joy" and that it was time to put the cameras back in the box.

This is particularly significant in Germany, where many fans are club members and therefore have genuine influence over the actions of their club and the governance of the game. Jochen Drees, the head of VAR operations in Germany, has however argued for refining the technology rather than removing it – a natural tendency, according to Gulavani.
VAR mission creep a symbol of technology's power
"VAR is a useful example of a broader societal pattern. As technology becomes more capable, we increasingly rely on it, but we also have to decide where its role should begin and end," he said.

"The appeal is understandable because AI can significantly improve efficiency and productivity. Tasks that once took hours can often be completed in minutes. At the same time, this expansion raises important questions about privacy, transparency, accountability, environmental costs, and where human judgment should remain central."
Is AI the better referee?
What will technology in sport look like in the future?
Sport without this technology is unlikely. Business, recruitment and event management are already finding ways to be more efficient thanks to the introduction of AI and other technologies.

As for VAR, perhaps a different system is required. At the U20 men's football World Cup last year, challenge cards, as seen in the NFL for example, were trialed. Coaches could ask for situations to be reviewed, reducing the interference of constant replays and slow-motion assessments. Reportedly, trialing of the approach, officially called Football Video Support (FVS), continues but it is likely seen as a cheaper alternative to the expensive VAR rather than a replacement.
"The key is to treat technology as decision support rather than decision replacement," Gulavani said. "

AI and technologies like VAR are good at processing large amounts of information quickly and consistently, but they cannot fully understand the context, intent, or nuance that many sporting decisions require. Human referees are still needed to interpret the Laws of the Game and exercise judgment in situations where there is no objectively 'correct' answer."

A return to a previous era seems unlikely, but the challenge is familiar. Can sport find a way to return technology to a supporting role rather than one that governs it to such an extent that it removes human engagement and emotion? If it can, perhaps those ripples will be felt beyond the white lines of sporting arenas.

articles.title: Organized crime and drug-related deaths rise Germany
articles.summary: Presenting its annual report for organized crime, the German police said that cocaine was a danger for the state and society, and that the cases of money laundering had increased.

image.caption: There were more drug-related deaths in Germany in 2025 than in the previous year Image: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

blocks.text: "We are experiencing a flood of cocaine in Germany," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, from the Christian Democrats (CDU), said earlier this week as a new police report was presented. "We are experiencing a record number of drug-related deaths. We are seeing children being exploited as criminals."

Standing alongside Dobrindt, Holger Münch, the president of the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), and Hendrik Streeck, the German government's drug and addiction commissioner, presented findings described as alarming.

blocks.caption: Holger Münch, Alexander Dobrindt and Hendrik Streeck presented the organized crime report this weekImage: Annette Riedl/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last year, 10 tons of cocaine were seized, two thirds of that amount in German ports. And 2,150 people lost their lives because of drug use, 13 more than in 2024.

Profits generated from drugs by international organized crime networks are often invested in real estate to conceal their origin. Münch said that 195 cases of money laundering, amounting to almost €1.4 billion (ca. $1.6 billion) had been investigated in 2025.
"They [the criminals] use their considerable financial clout to bribe and to exert influence," he said. "And they launder the money and funnel it into the legal economic system."
He added that the most widely used drug was cocaine and that it posed a threat to the state, the economy and society as a whole.
'There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure'
"It is not only the state that is being damaged," said Streeck. "Above all, it is people who are being damaged."
About 83% of the drug-related deaths concerned men, whose average age was 41.
"They are all customers of a market that deals in deadly substances and is driven by violence, environmental destruction, extortion and exploitation," said Streeck, who trained as a doctor.

He insisted that there should be zero tolerance for those who profited from addiction and zero indifference to those suffering from it. His focus is on preventative measures, which include a public awareness campaign about the impact on health and the environment.

He explained that in some countries, rainforests were being cleared to make way for cocaine production. Streek pointed out that toxic substances used for processing the drug, such as kerosene or battery acid, ended up in the soil and water. Farmers and their families were blackmailed. He lamented the fact that cocaine had become more popular in Germany.
"There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure," the drug and addiction commissioner stated.
Cocaine, Crime, Cartels: Can Europe fight back?
Digitalization of drugs trade
Streeck added that the situation had changed significantly in recent years and the market had gone digital.
"Dealers are no longer on the street corner; they're on the phone. For example, people can order so-called 'cocaine taxis' [cars that deliver drugs to any location] via QR code," he said.

"What is particularly alarming is that criminal groups are recruiting minors through social media or gaming platforms," he added. "Organized criminals look for recruits in the places where young people spend their free time."

Münch noted that this development posed a particular challenge for German and international law enforcement agencies. He said that, more and more, the cliched image of organized crime — discretion, isolation and closed structures — was a thing of the past. The fact that people can purchase criminal services on the dark web represents a paradigm shift, according to Münch: "It's not just a question of who commits a crime, but of who ordered it, who financed it, who is profiting from it?"
Moreover, there is a suspicion on the part of investigators that state actors are increasingly involved in opaque crime activities, launching attacks as "hybrid threats."
Münch said that "money laundering, corruption and violence can contribute to social destabilization."
Risky business: European dock workers helping drug cartels

In 2025, there were about 600 investigations into cases of organized crime in Germany, which has been the average for the past five years. The German police considers one of its major successes to be the shutdown of the Archetyp Market, an online drug marketplace on the darknet. Its administrator was arrested in June 2025. He had overseen the sale of cocaine, heroin, cannabis and other drugs, amounting to 250 million. When the platform was shut down there were 3,200 registered sellers and 612,000 customer accounts according to the police.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: At least 3 dead from school shooting in South Cotabato
articles.summary: The Department of Education confirmed on Friday, September 18, a reported shooting incident at Banga National High School in Banga, South Cotabato.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 2:40pm
Content warning: School shooting

MANILA, Philippines (Updated 5:10 p.m.) — A shooting incident at Banga National High School in Banga, South Cotabato, on Friday, September 18, has resulted in at least three fatalities and six injuries.
This was confirmed by South Cotabato Governor Reynald Tamayo.
The Department of Education earlier confirmed the on-campus attack and said it was "deeply concerned" by the "reported shooting incident" at Banga National High School.

The department said it is currently coordinating with its Schools Division Office and Regional Office, local authorities, and law enforcement "to verify the circumstances and provide necessary assistance."
"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers, and school personnel," DepEd said.
DepEd said it is ready to give psychological first aid and mental health and psychosocial support to those affected.
It urged the public to stay calm and stop sharing unverified information while authorities investigate.

In a separate statement, DepEd's Region XII office urged the public to immediately cease the distribution of videos of the "incident in Banga" to "respect the victims and their families." It said that sharing the material would cause trauma and violate the privacy of victims.

Meanwhile, the Philippine Red Cross said preliminary reports, which are subject to verification, indicated that six injured individuals were transported to Dantom Doctors Hospital and South Cotabato Provincial Hospital. It also reported one fatality and said the suspected shooter was reportedly among the injured and was a student.
The public school sits in Barangay Benitez, Banga, and offers both junior and senior high school.
This comes less than three months after two students opened fire at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City on June 22, killing at least three schoolmates and wounding about 20 others.
On August 18, a shooting broke out at the junior high school building of Ateneo de Zamboanga University. A student armed with two pistols shot dead a schoolmate.
The Learners TeleSafe Contact Center Helpline may be reached through #33733 (#DEPED), 0945-175-9777, email [email protected] and Viber.

articles.title: Russia votes for new parliament in controlled elections
articles.summary: Russia is holding elections for the State Duma for the first time since Moscow sent troops into Ukraine in 2022. The party of President Vladimir Putin is expected to win the highly controlled affair.

image.caption: The three-day election ends on Sunday eveningImage: Tatiana Meel/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russians began casting ballots on Friday to elect a new lower house of parliament, kicking off a three-day vote that President Vladimir Putin's party is all but guaranteed to win.
This is the first such election being held since Moscow sent troops to invade Ukraine in February 2022.
Parties that support Putin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition is barred from taking part.

blocks.caption: Russia's opposition party, Yabloko, was banished from the party list last monthImage: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Despite expectations of Putin's easy win, the elections are widely being viewed as a referendum on the continuation of his military campaign — now in its fifth year.

The polls are taking place at a time when public sentiment is starting to shift against the war over rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.
Meanwhile, Putin has called the vote a "collective contribution to Russia's victory against Ukraine.
Vote for control
More than 110 million Russians are eligible to vote for 450 members of the lower house of the Russian Parliament, known as the State Duma.
Putin's United Russia party currently controls over two-thirds of the seats and is expected to retain its dominance, allowing it to continue the military campaign despite ebbing public support.
The Kamchatka peninsula and Chukotka were the first of Russia's 11 time zones to begin voting on Friday.
Polls will remain open until 1800 GMT on Sunday.

Voting is being held for the first time in the Russia-occupied Ukrainian territories of Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, against Kyiv's wishes. The Black Sea peninsula of Crimea, annexed by Moscow in 2014, is participating for the second time.
While voters select their parliamentarians, members of regional parliaments will also be elected in eight regions.

articles.title: NUJP, journalists lament loss of media watchdog as CMFR writes 30
articles.summary: Media practitioners and journalist groups have conveyed bittersweet messages of sadness and respect as the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR) writes 30--an industry term that…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 2:22pm

Media practitioners and journalist groups have conveyed bittersweet messages of sadness and respect as the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR) writes 30—an industry term that indicates that a story is complete.
The CMFR announced that it would cease operations on September 30, after 37 years of serving an independently funded vanguard of a free Filipino press.
The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) said it regretted the pending closure of CMFR.
"Its work has helped the press hold power to account while also reminding journalists that the freedom we exercise carries with it a responsibility to the public," the NUJP wrote.

"The loss of a watchdog that watches over the watchdogs is a profound blow to Philippine journalism, leaving a void in an industry that needs accountability. At a time when the press faces mounting pressures from various interests, the absence of CMFR's independent voice will be deeply felt," the union added.
More journalists have also expressed their sorrow following the CMFR's closure, with many lauding CMFR founder Melinda Quintos de Jesus.
Presidential Task Force on Media Security Executive Director Joe Torres, who formerly served as editor-in-chief of GMA News Online, extended his gratitude to the CMFR.

"Started in journalism in 1989, the year CMFR started. The organization has been a great help in the formation of many journalists of my time. Maraming salamat, CMFR, Ma'am Melinda, at sa lahat na mga kaibigan at nakasama sa Center," Torres said in a comment on the post.
Legacy
Former Business World editor-in-chief and now PLDT communications division chief Roby Alampay also lauded the watchdog.

"Your legacy and the impact of Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility will live on. We are all grateful — and now collectively responsible to ensure that it be so. Maraming salamat sa lahat nang bumuo at bumuhay sa CMFR at kanyang adhikain!” Alampay said.
NUJP Chair Jonathan de Santos, who serves as ABS-CBN deputy editor, also thanked the CMFR in a separate statement.

"My informal journ school whose standards I aspire to and sometimes met. Thank you for your decades of service, guidance, praise and scolding, and hope in journalism in the Philippines," De Santos said.
Sports journalist Rey Joble thanked CMFR for standing with him during a plagiarism issue, wherein portions of his work were copied into another article.
“Your legacy lives on. But allow me to thank you, CMFR, for standing by me at the height of my plagiarism issue 15 years ago. It was a life-changing moment,” Joble said.
TV5 journalist Ed Lingao, meanwhile, put it simply: "CMFR writes -30-."
Standing up for rights
Meanwhile, the In Defense of Human Rights and Dignity Movement (iDefend) group expressed sadness over the CMFR's impending closure.
iDEFEND said that the CMFR was there to stand by the truth during former president Rodrigo Duterte's bloody war on drugs.

"Ang inyong pagtindig sa karapatang pantao at demokrasya ay malaking kontribusyon sa pagpapanagot sa nagdaang administrasyon. Mula sa hanay ng iDefend, pagpupugay at pasasalamat CMFR!" the group said.
(Your stance on human rights and democracy was a big contributor to holding the previous administration accountable. From iDefend, recognition and gratitude.)
— VDV, GMA News
