articles.title: Philippines' media watchdog CMFR to close after 37 years
articles.summary: Post-EDSA press freedom watchdog ends 37 years of operations on Sept. 30.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 2:07pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility, a fixture of Philippine journalism's post-dictatorship rebuilding, will shut down on September 30 after 37 years, citing mounting difficulty securing funds for its operations.

CMFR announced the closure Friday, September 18, citing the decision of its board. With it ends the work of one of the country's most established media watchdogs and an institution that helped shape professional and ethical standards in Philippine journalism.

"Philippine and international funding support has sustained the work of CMFR; but multiple factors have affected the funding environment, making it difficult for CMFR to secure the necessary funds for its operations," the organization said.

Established in 1989 by journalist Melinda Quintos de Jesus, three years after the People Power uprising ended the Marcos dictatorship, CMFR was created as the Philippine press rebuilt its freedoms and institutions after 14 years of authoritarian rule.
Its founding premise joined two concerns that would define much of its work: defending press freedom from outside interference while demanding greater responsibility from the press itself.
Over nearly four decades, CMFR became a persistent monitor of both.

It documented killings, threats and attacks against journalists, tracked impunity in media murders and regularly assessed the state of press freedom. At the same time, it scrutinized news coverage for accuracy, fairness, balance, context and sourcing, often publicly calling out lapses by news organizations.

That role placed CMFR in an unusual position in the industry. It defended journalists against repression while arguing that press freedom could be sustained only by stronger professional practice and self-regulation.
Building standards after dictatorship
CMFR began monitoring Philippine media in 1990, developing what became the Philippine Journalism Review and later PJR Reports into vehicles for peer review, accountability and continuing education.

Through media monitoring, training programs and published ethical guidelines, CMFR sought to establish common standards in a profession where routes into journalism, training and newsroom practices varied widely.

Its 2007 ethics manual was published as an effort to further professionalize Philippine journalism, linking ethical practice with competence and laying out guidance on accuracy, conflicts of interest, privacy and coverage of crises, crime, war, terrorism, women and children.

CMFR also organized training for working journalists, developed reporting manuals and established press councils intended to give members of the public a way to raise grievances against media without immediately turning to the courts.

PJR Reports became a regular forum for evaluating the performance of Philippine news organizations and a reference for journalism schools. CMFR described the publication as a mechanism for self-evaluation and correction, and as a model of media self-regulation.

The organization also spent two decades administering the Jaime V. Ongpin Awards for Excellence in Journalism, which recognized investigative and explanatory reporting and helped establish benchmarks for sourcing, verification, fairness, accuracy and technical proficiency.
Its next iteration, the Jaime V. Ongpin Journalism Seminar, annually selects journalists commended for their coverage of critical issues affecting Filipinos.
CMFR's ethics manual and other publications also became reference materials in universities, while its seminars regularly brought working journalists together with students and faculty.
Watching the watchdogs
As a watchdog, CMFR was frequently unsparing toward the industry it sought to protect.
Its media monitoring examined not only attacks on journalists but failures within journalism itself, including weak sourcing, lack of context, sensationalism and ethical lapses.
That combination of advocacy and criticism reflected an argument embedded in CMFR's work since its founding: that the credibility of the press was itself part of the defense of press freedom.
The organization also became a repository of data on attacks against journalists.

Its reports, often produced with other media organizations and press-freedom groups, documented journalist killings, legal harassment, red-tagging, surveillance, censorship and other threats across successive administrations.
CMFR's reports and alerts also circulated through international press-freedom networks, giving its documentation a role beyond the Philippine media industry.
An institution of the post-1986 press

The organization's lifespan covered markedly different periods for the Philippine press, from the democratic opening after Ferdinand Marcos Sr.'s dictatorship through successive political crises, the rise of digital media, the collapse of traditional advertising models and renewed pressure on journalists.
CMFR described those 37 years as a mission carried out through "widely differing political environments and the diverse challenges they presented."

Its closure comes as the economics supporting journalism and media-development institutions have grown more difficult, while Philippine news organizations continue to face questions of financial sustainability, safety and public trust.

In its farewell statement, CMFR and its executive director thanked its past and present staff, journalists and news organizations, embassies, schools, students and civil society groups that had supported its work.
"We are truly grateful," De Jesus said. "Please accept our best wishes."

articles.title: Revealed: How Russia use mobile ‘super-app’ Max to spy on its citizens
articles.summary:
Research shows tens of millions of people are being forced to use platform that amounts to ‘backdoor’ on their device

Over the past 18 months, tens of millions of Russians have been forced…

blocks.text: Over the past 18 months, tens of millions of Russians have been forced to install a new app on their phones – a violet-blue button designed for messaging and payments, called Max.

Authorities have touted it as a patriotic alternative to Telegram and WhatsApp; Russian glitterati have promoted it in rap videos and comic routines. This summer, it became the country’s most-used messaging app.
It is a product of VKontakte, the Russian social media company, which is deeply entangled with the Russian state. The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly owns an indirect stake in Max.

Max is Russia’s version of a “super-app,” combining an ecosystem of services into a single platform. It is a container for a number of “mini-apps” that now facilitate everyday life in Russia – banking apps, a messaging service that aims to replace Telegram, and apps for essential government services. The best-known super-app in the world is WeChat, China’s everything platform which facilitates the state’s social controls.
But while WeChat was developed over decades, in step with China’s other internet controls, Max has been imposed on a population that once had mostly-free internet access.

blocks.caption: Max is described as ‘a blueprint any government can follow’ towards digital authoritarianism. Photograph: Contributor/Getty Images

blocks.text: Now, forensic research has revealed a fuller picture of Max’s powerful surveillance capabilities. These amount to a “backdoor” into its entire mini-app ecosystem on every user’s device, said Roya Ensafi, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Michigan.

“We have studied Russia’s escalation of internet control for the past decade,” said Ensafi. “What Max provides is the cleverest and also the scariest tactic by authoritarian governments” to surveil their citizens.
Max is “a blueprint any government can follow” towards digital authoritarianism, said Ensafi.
It represents the cutting edge of what governments such as Iran, Kazakhstan and India may soon try to achieve.

Ensafi’s team were able to download the version of the app used in Russia. They found that Max can screenshot users’ devices – and the contents of its mini-apps – without their knowledge. It can access all the information stored in these mini-apps, their messages and payments. It can impersonate its users without them knowing.
It can even inject code into mini-apps – which would mean, said Ensafi, that the Russian government could use Max to launch cyberattacks.

Their research adds new clarity into an ongoing debate on Max’s surveillance capabilities. Crucially, said Ensafi, it cannot break into apps like Telegram and WhatsApp, if users have these installed. However, Russia has banned both.

Many Russians working in or around state institutions have in effect been forced to use Max. Officials and public-sector employees, university students, teachers and even schoolchildren have all faced pressure to move their communications on to the platform.
One schoolteacher in Moscow said staff at their school were ordered to switch to Max after instructions from the city authorities.

“The school director called us in last March and told us directly: from now on, everything is on Max. That included chats with parents, sending out homework and other school communication,” the teacher said.
“There isn’t really an option to say no, so in the end you just use the app,” they added.

blocks.caption: The Russian State Duma deputy, Sergey Boyarsky, demonstrating an age verification system using the Max app at a supermarket in February. Photograph: Contributor/Getty Images

blocks.text: Daniil, a university student in St Petersburg, said he reluctantly downloaded Max shortly before the start of the academic year after being told students would be denied access to university buildings or dormitories without a QR code generated through the app.
He said he had concerns about the app’s security and privacy, but felt he had little choice if he wanted to continue accessing campus.

Among Russia’s elite, use of Max often appears to be largely performative, with Telegram and Signal still widely used for day-to-day communication, according to several well-connected figures and prominent businesspeople.
One person in the Kremlin’s inner circle said he and several friends had bought second phones solely to install Max, while continuing to use their main devices and preferred messaging apps as before.
“It’s all for show. No one in politics really uses it,” the person said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Max has yet to replace Telegram as a major source of news for Russians. Public channels – used by media outlets, bloggers and officials to broadcast news and commentary to large audiences – remain far less developed on Max, where only a small number have built audiences comparable to the biggest channels on Telegram.

Several Max users contacted by the Guardian said the app closely resembles Telegram, long Russia’s most popular messaging platform, in its design and functionality, but concerns about privacy and surveillance were widespread.
“Using Max feels like you never quite know who else might be watching,” said Nikolai, a 34-year-old consultant in Moscow.
While the app looked modern and slick, Nikolai said there was always something slightly sinister about using it.
“You end up using it more and more because the alternatives are becoming harder to access. But it still doesn’t feel right.”

Russia’s success in rapidly pushing out Max should be a “wake-up call”, said Ensafi. China reached its current state of digital authoritarianism over the course of 35 years. But Russia has imposed these sweeping restrictions – shepherding people on to a state-controlled internet – in just a decade.
“The world is changing, the infrastructure of private communication is changing – and the assault by authoritarian governments is very aggressive,” she said.
Max and VKontakte were approached for comment.

articles.title: Chinese vessel rams PH ship on fuel subsidy mission near Palawan
articles.summary: Chinese vessel rams PH ship on fuel subsidy mission near Palawan

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 1:56pm

A China Coast Guard (CCG) vessel rammed a Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) ship that was delivering fuel subsidies to Filipino fishermen in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) on Friday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said.
PCG spokesperson for WPS Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said CCG vessel 21585 rammed the BRP Datu Magat Salamat while the Philippine vessel was carrying out its maritime patrol and fuel subsidy mission.
Tarriela said that at 11:04 a.m., the Chinese vessel reportedly cut across the stern of the BFAR vessel at a distance of only about 10 meters.
At 11:13 a.m., while the BRP Datu Magat Salamat was maintaining its course, the Chinese vessel repeated the maneuver and made contact with the BFAR vessel, striking it.

A China Coast Guard (CCG) vessel rammed a Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) ship that was delivering fuel subsidies to Filipino fishermen in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) on Friday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said. 🎥: PCG @gmanews pic.twitter.com/5F8jzM7t9H— Joviland Rita (@jovilandxrita) September 18, 2026

The Philippine vessel sustained damage on its starboard side including the bent, broken, and detached; deformed metal stanchions and support structures deformed; and displaced deck fixtures and equipment displaced, with debris scattered across the deck.
After the collision, CCG-21585 conducted another dangerous maneuver, passing dead astern at a distance of only about five meters, according to Tarriela.
GMA News Online has reached out to the Chinese Embassy for comment but it has yet to reply as of posting time.
The incident occurred around 6.36 nautical miles north-northwest of Abad Santos Shoal and about 54 nautical miles from Palawan's coast, within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
PCG Commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan has directed PCG surface and air assets to proceed to the location of the BFAR vessel to provide assistance and ensure the safety of its crew.

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago including Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: South Korea will not send military to support US war on Iran, defying Trump pressure
articles.summary:
Seoul resolves recent speculation over sending military to strait of Hormuz, saying ‘there won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war’

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has…

blocks.text: South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has said he will ⁠not deploy the military to the ⁠Middle East in a way ​that could draw the country into conflict, resisting calls from Donald Trump to support his war in Iran.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee said at a ⁠news conference on Friday. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”

However, Lee added that he was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region. South Korea maintains a naval presence off the coast of Somalia as part of an anti-piracy mission.
“[It] is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to ​protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of ‌our people,” he said.

Trump has criticised Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war ‌and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the US ally.
South Korea’s government has been reviewing a ‌possible military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, although the idea is proving unpopular domestically.

Asked about progress in reaching an agreement with the US on Seoul’s US investment commitments under its trade deal with Washington, Lee said concern over the commercial viability of the package was the main sticking point.
Lee said there were elements that were difficult for Seoul to accept, but that the two sides were nearing an agreement.
South Korea committed last year to invest $350bn in US manufacturing in return for Washington lowering tariffs on Korean imports to 15%.
Seoul this week postponed ‌a parliamentary briefing on the investment plans, which is expected to take place next week instead.

The South Korean president also said it was possible that a meeting could take place in the coming months between Trump and the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but many factors needed ​to align for that to happen.
“What’s clear is that President Trump wants talks, and I want him to as well, and we’re continuing coordination to make dialogue between the North and the US possible,” he said.

North Korean state media has so far remained largely silent on the repeated calls from Trump for such a meeting. Trump has been pushing aides for a meeting with Kim as soon as the autumn, the Wall Street Journal has reported.

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 1:40pm

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said Friday several Chinese vessels were spotted during the recent distribution of fuel subsidy and food packs to Filipino fishermen at Bajo de Masinloc, also known as Scarborough Shoal.
In a statement, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said the following Chinese ships were seen Thursday in the area:

items: one People's Liberation Army Navy (PLA-N) warship
three China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels
three Chinese maritime militia vessels

blocks.text: Tarriela said the Chinese warship issued a radio challenge to the PCG's Piper Navajo aircraft, which responded by asserting that it was conducting a lawful maritime patrol within Philippine maritime zones, in accordance with international law.

"The continued presence of Chinese maritime forces in and around BDM, a traditional fishing ground of Filipino fisherfolk, remains inconsistent with the 2016 Arbitral Award and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)," Tarriela said.
"The Award affirmed that Bajo de Masinloc is a traditional fishing ground of Filipino fishermen and that China unlawfully prevented them from fishing there," he added.

Tarriela said the PCG conducted a maritime domain awareness flight over Bajo de Masinloc in support of the ongoing Kadiwa ng Bagong Bayaning Mangingisda mission led by the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR).
A total of 35 Filipino fishing boats were sighted to receive diesel and food packs.
Bajo de Masinloc is located 124 nautical miles off Masinloc, Zambales, and is considered within the Philippines' 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country's claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago including Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Indonesia gets its first aircraft carrier amid debate over cost and military ambitions
articles.summary:
The gift from Italy has sparked fierce debate among defence analysts and opposition politicians who question its true cost and purpose

Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a…

blocks.text: Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelagic nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities.

The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony.

Italy in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the south-east Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.

blocks.caption: Indonesia’s first aircraft carrier, the ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi (C), arrives at Tanjung Priok port in Jakarta. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: The transfer would make Indonesia only the second country in south-east Asia with a carrier in its fleet. The first was Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet, which was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump-jets.

The carrier will be formally commissioned into the Indonesian Navy next week as the KRI Gajah Mada, named after the famed 14th-century Majapahit-era military leader, whose campaigns and vision of a unified archipelago have made him one of Indonesia’s most celebrated historical figures.

Defence development was one of the top priorities for president Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries.

But the Garibaldi acquisition has sparked a fierce debate among defence analysts, economists and opposition politicians who question whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship while facing mounting fiscal pressures at home.

Indonesia’s finance ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier program in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16tn rupiah (about $900m).

blocks.caption: The aircraft carrier ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi sailing near Bangka Belitung island.  Photograph: Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet Command Public Relations Office/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across its thousands of islands.

Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of south-east Asia with hazardous haze.

Prabowo said the carrier could accommodate up to 10 medium-sized helicopters, including aircraft with capabilities comparable to the Black Hawk and Mi-17, and could carry large quantities of water and be deployed to areas with large numbers of fire hotspots.

He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters, which are common in Indonesia, a nation that sits in the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”

blocks.caption: The through-deck aviation cruiser class ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi docks in Indonesia. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster-relief needs.

The acquisition comes as Indonesia’s economy faces growing fiscal pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding a free nutritious meals program – which has been tainted by multiple food poisoning incidents – and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenues and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects.

blocks.caption: Experts have warned that operating a carrier is extremely costly. Photograph: Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet Command Public Relations Office/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

He said policymakers must weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the Navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure.

Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints.

“The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.”

blocks.caption: Indonesian defence minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin on the ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers are not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters.
“Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said.

But he added that if Indonesia is seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions.”

articles.title: Aztec manuscript returns to Mexico after two centuries, on loan
articles.summary: For years, Mexico has demanded the return of a treasured manuscript. Now the Aztec relic is back home from France — but on loan.

image.caption: The Azcatitlan Codex will remain on display in Mexico City until DecemberImage: Carl De Souza/AFP

blocks.text: The Azcatitlan Codex, a rare and prized manuscript that recounts the history of the Aztecs in vibrant pictograms, has returned to Mexico for the first time since 1840. It went on display in Mexico City on Thursday.

The codex is a 16th-century artifact and regarded as one of the most important visual records of Aztec history. It records the founding of the Aztec capital to its fall after the subsequent arrival of Spanish conquistadores.
It arrived in Mexico on loan from France's Bibliotheque Nationale, where it has been since 1898. The temporary loan is occurring as the two nations celebrate 200 years of diplomatic ties.

blocks.caption: In return for the Azcatitlan Codex, Mexico will loan a different historical artifact to FranceImage: Carl De Souza/AFP

blocks.text: Reunited with history

As two folios from the document went on display inside a glass case at the National Museum of Anthropology, Mexican Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco said the exhibition was about "reuniting a population with its (collective) memory."
The pictograms "represent our history, the written voice of our ancestors, and the deep root of our identity," he said, speaking at the inauguration.

blocks.caption: The codex was created in Mexico by an indigenous craftsman from the Otomi people Image: Carl De Souza/AFP

blocks.text: Mexico has demanded the treasured artifact be returned for years.
Members of an indigenous group reacted ecstatically to the display. "They hid our history from us, they stole it!" Emilia Mendoza of the Hnahnu community said at the opening exhibition.
"This is a battle won, a first step toward the restitution of these books that reside in other countries," she said.
What's in the Azcatitlan Codex?
Made up of Mesoamerican pictograms with European writing, the codex is divided into three parts.

It traces the Mexica's migration from Aztlan — the mythical birthplace of the Aztec civilization — to the founding of Tenochtitlan. That's the capital of the Aztec empire and is present day Mexico City.
The document also depicts the succession of the city's rulers, the arrival of the Spanish and the subsequent evangelization, according to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History.
All of this has been rendered in the codex in vibrant reds, blues, greens and yellows, depicting warriors in feathered headdresses and showcasing ritual acts in pyramid temples.

More than five centuries have now passed since Tenochtitlan fell to Hernan Cortes, the leader of the invading Spanish forces. As most histories of invasion go, Cortez and his allies looted and razed the city after conquest, ushering in three centuries of Spanish domination.
Historic megacity — the legendary Aztec capital

"These codices are extremely important to us because they continue to give us identity and value as human beings during these very special times we are experiencing," said ​Maria Eugenia Castaneda, representative of the Mexica peoples. "They elevate our morale, our customs, our culture, and our sense of who we are."
According to Mexican historians, an indigenous craftsman from the Otomi people created the codex.

The document will remain on display until December. As part of the exchange, Mexico will loan France another important historical document — the Codex Boturini — which also depicts the migration of the Aztec people to the Mexican valley.

articles.title: Russians go to polls against backdrop of Ukraine war and Putin’s tightening grip
articles.summary:
President’s United Russia party faces no meaningful opposition after liberal anti-war party barred from ballot

Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly…

blocks.text: Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result.

Vladimir Putin’s United Russia is expected to extend the grip on parliament it has held for 23 years, alongside a handful of nominal opposition parties that reliably vote with the Kremlin on the issues that matter. The three-day vote begins on Friday, with results expected after polls close on Sunday.

For all the predictability of the outcome, the first Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is taking place against the backdrop of a war that, once distant for many Russians, is increasingly intruding into everyday life.

Swarms of Ukrainian drones have struck oil refineries, factories and logistics hubs across Russia over the summer, while polling has pointed to growing anxiety about the course of the fighting and what may still lie ahead.
Against that backdrop, the Kremlin has tightened its grip further.
Last month, the authorities barred Yabloko, the liberal anti-war party, from the ballot, removing the only political force remaining in Russia that was openly challenging the invasion of Ukraine.

That leaves a handful of other parties, from the Communists to the far-right Liberal Democrats, which together form what is known in Russia as the “systemic opposition”: groups permitted to criticise the authorities at the margins, but which fall into line with United Russia on issues that matter to the Kremlin.

blocks.caption: A Russian Communist party rally in downtown Moscow on Thursday. Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/EPA

blocks.text: For years, they have served as a political safety valve, giving voters somewhere to register discontent without posing a serious threat to the ruling party’s dominance. But even by the diminished standards of Russian politics, these parliamentary campaigns have been strikingly lifeless.

“In most elections, candidates compete for attention. In Russia this year, many are doing the opposite,” said Farida Rustamova, a political analyst and founder of the independent Vlast newsletter. “No one wants to come into the spotlight or discuss anything sensitive.”
Most candidates have barely campaigned at all, she noted.
Televised debates have at times taken place in half-empty studios because politicians failed to turn up, producing awkward clips that quickly became memes online.

blocks.caption: A campaign worker handing out promotional materials for United Russia in Yaroslavl. Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/Reuters

blocks.text: United Russia’s campaign videos have leaned heavily on low-budget AI, with few memorable slogans or promises. None of the parties has dared to address the growing questions surrounding the continuing war that increasingly dominate private conversations.

“The Kremlin is deliberately keeping the election low-key, as greater interest would not benefit them. They don’t want to discuss difficult issues and just [want to] get it over with,” said a person close to the Kremlin, speaking on condition of anonymity.
after newsletter promotion
By keeping the election subdued, Moscow hoped to depress turnout among disaffected and independent-minded voters while ensuring its own supporters made it to the polls, said Rustamova.
Yabloko’s exclusion followed the same logic.

Several observers believe that officials had initially expected the party to receive a negligible result, demonstrating how little support remained for an explicitly anti-war platform. But when polling instead suggested growing support for the party, the authorities removed it from the ballot rather than risk an unscripted result.

blocks.caption: A candidate for Russia's liberal Yabloko party handing out flyers in Moscow. Photograph: Yulia Morozova/Reuters

blocks.text: Vladimir Gelman, a professor of Russian politics at the University of Helsinki, said another purpose of the elections was to provide the Kremlin with a continuing source of legitimacy and reinforce the impression that there was broad public consent behind the political system and the war.
“Even though these elections are neither free nor fair, they are still the only source of legitimacy,” he said.

In a televised address before the vote this week, Putin explicitly linked participation in the election to the war in Ukraine, presenting voting as a demonstration of unity in the face of outside pressure.

“Your choice and your will will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory and love for our homeland,” Putin said.
Putin himself secured another six-year term in the 2024 presidential election, with genuine opposition barred from the ballot, extending his rule until at least 2030.

blocks.caption: Putin recording his video address ​to the nation. Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP

blocks.text: For many Russians, however, the election’s greater significance lies not in the result, but in what follows.

With Moscow’s troops making little progress at high cost in Ukraine, rumours of another large-scale mobilisation have spread across the country. The fear is that once the election is safely out of the way and a compliant new Duma is installed, the Kremlin will have greater freedom to pursue unpopular measures it has so far avoided.

The anxiety has already prompted some young men to leave the country, hoping to wait out any new mobilisation – scenes that carry echoes of September 2022, when hundreds of thousands of Russians fled after Putin announced the first wartime draft.

The person close to the Kremlin said several friends had sent their sons abroad in recent weeks, a sign, he said, that even among those with access to the system, few are certain what will happen after the voting.
Putin has sought to calm those fears. In recent weeks, he has twice dismissed suggestions that a new mobilisation is imminent.

But those reassurances have not been enough for some men, including Dmitry, who flew to Yerevan, Armenia last week. “I’ll just wait a few weeks after the elections,” he said, adding that he felt the risk of a new mobilisation was too high to ignore. “Let’s see if anything changes after the vote.”

articles.title: Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has lobbied the US for years to buy F35s, the world's most advanced fighter jet.

blocks.text: Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.
He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party".
Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia.
They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries.
The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives".
It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region".
"The proposed ⁠sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military ⁠balance in the region," the state department added.
Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November.
The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history".
The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin.
This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets.
However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May, external that it would procure another F-35 squadron.
This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post, external.
Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m.
Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.
Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its ⁠relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered.
The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen.
The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said.
Additional reporting by Sareen Habeshian

articles.title: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
articles.summary: The White House removed Larsson's Midnight Sun from one of its reels after the artist called the clip "dehumanising".

blocks.text: Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.

The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.
The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun".

In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.
Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.
In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".
Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people."
"The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future".

"It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.
Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life.
White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.

Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda".

Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

articles.title: What Philippines' aging population means, and what can be done
articles.summary: Fewer Filipinos are being born. What comes next?

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 8:50am
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines' fertility rate has fallen to 1.7 children per woman, sharpening concerns that a smaller future workforce will have to support a rapidly aging population.

The Commission on Population and Development (CPD) warned that persistently low fertility could eventually weaken the country's base of workers, taxpayers and contributors to social protection systems, while increasing demand for healthcare and other services for older Filipinos.

The country's total fertility rate, or the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime based on current fertility patterns, dropped from 1.9 in 2022 to 1.7 in 2025, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.
That is well below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman.

Mylin Mirasol Quiray, information management and communications division chief of the CPD, said Thursday that the effects would become more consequential as today's smaller cohorts eventually enter the labor force.

"Low fertility rate can be a hindrance to economic progress kasi mas magiging kaunti 'yung ating mga tao na ipinapanganak na maaaring mag-earn ng money, mag-spend, mag-save," Quiray said on "Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon" radio, citing the International Monetary Fund.
(A low fertility rate can be a hindrance to economic progress because fewer people will be born who can earn money, spend and save.)
She said the more immediate concern is the country's future contributor base, as fewer births today eventually translate into fewer workers.
"'Yung declining fertility maaaring ma-weaken 'yung contributory base natin, which is fewer workers na puwedeng mapanganak," she said, citing the Philippine Institute for Development Studies.
(Declining fertility may weaken our contributory base, meaning fewer workers will be born.)
Philippines getting older
The shift is already visible in the country's age structure.
The 2024 Census of Population found that Filipinos aged 65 and older numbered 7.4 million, or 6.6% of the household population, up from 5.4% in 2020.
The country's median age also rose to 27.7 years in 2024 from 25.3 in 2020 and 24.3 in 2015, according to the PSA.
Meanwhile, Filipinos aged 60 and older reached 11.42 million, equivalent to 10.2% of the household population.
State-run research center PIDS has projected that people aged 65 and older could account for about 7.6% of the population by 2030, as the country moves further into an aging demographic structure.
Quiray said an older population would mean greater demand for public services.
"Kapag aging population na tayo, mas maraming pangangailangan 'no, sa health services, social services," she said.
(As our population ages, there will be greater demand for health services and social services.)
She said the government would need to invest earlier in health and human development so Filipinos can remain active and healthy as they age.

Recent PIDS research has warned that below-replacement fertility, combined with population aging and a potentially smaller labor force, could increase pressure on social security systems and government revenues over the longer term.
Demographic dividend still open
The demographic pressure is not immediate, however.
The Philippines still has a large working-age population. In 2024, about 74.95 million Filipinos, or 66.7% of the household population, were aged 15 to 64.
The overall dependency ratio improved to about 50 dependents for every 100 working-age Filipinos in 2024, from 57 in 2020.
Quiray said the current labor force remains large enough to support children and older dependents.
"Mas marami pa rin naman tayong workers dito sa ating population ngayon na puwedeng suportahan 'yung mga bata at saka matatanda," she said.
(We still have more workers in our population who can support children and older people.)
That gives the country time to prepare for the longer-term consequences of lower fertility.

PIDS likewise says the Philippines' demographic dividend remains open, but argues that policy must increasingly shift from controlling population growth toward building human capital and preparing for population aging.
That includes investing more heavily in early childhood development, education, healthcare and family support while the country still has a relatively large share of working-age people.
Not simply about having more children
The decline in fertility also poses a more complicated policy challenge than simply encouraging Filipinos to have bigger families.
CPD said family planning policy should continue to allow people to decide whether, when and how many children they want, rather than seek a particular fertility target.

"Kailangan pa rin natin talaga na mag-family planning para 'yung mga gustong manganak, kung kailan nila gustong manganak, ay mangyayari at kung hindi nila gustong magkaanak ay mangyayari pa rin para sa kanila," Quiray said.
(We still need family planning so that those who want to have children can do so when they choose, while those who do not want children can also make that choice.)

Modern contraceptive use among Filipino women has continued to increase, according to Quiray, rising from 41.8% in 2022 to 44.5% in 2025. Use of traditional methods such as withdrawal and the calendar method fell from 16.5% to 14.1% over the same period.
PIDS has also found that falling fertility does not necessarily mean all Filipino couples want fewer children.

Poorer households continue to have more children than they intend in some cases, while wealthier couples may have fewer children than they want, pointing to different barriers including employment insecurity, housing, caregiving responsibilities and the cost of raising a family.

articles.title: Almost 50 dead in Nigeria after drinking alcohol suspected to contain methanol
articles.summary:
Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated

At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving…

blocks.text: At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving treatment in southern Nigeria after consuming a locally brewed alcoholic concoction suspected to contain methanol, officials said on Thursday.

Banji Ajaka, Ondo state’s commissioner for health, said the cases had been reported in the Odigbo and Irele local government areas. A total of 182 people are believed to have been affected and some are being treated in the hospital, he said.
“I took like two shots and I went out on Friday. On Saturday, I noticed that I could not see,” 32-year-old Sola Adebayo told the local TVC News channel from a hospital bed.
Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated.

“This thing happened rapidly. Once they consume, depending on the quantity, the kidneys will pack up, the eyes will go, the brain will be damaged,” Ajaka told The Associated Press, speaking about the drink.

Ondo state police spokesperson Abayomi Jimoh said in a statement that 15 people were arrested in connection with the incident, including one allegedly “involved in the production of substances suspected to contain methanol and is currently assisting the police with investigations.”
Locals told the AP they suspected a popular herbal drink with high alcohol content, known as “Monkey Tail,” was mixed with methanol, causing the deaths.

A trader who sells the concoction in Odigbo, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of being arrested, told the AP there are two versions of Monkey Tail: an original, safe version, and another version which is unsafe.
Local media reports said the first death was reported nearly two weeks ago.

Nigeria’s National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control is now enforcing a nationwide ban on alcohol in sachets and small plastic containers, which it said are easily accessible to children and young people.

articles.title: US court sentences ex-Syrian official who ran notorious ‘punishment wing’ to 60 years
articles.summary:
Samir Ousman al-Sheikh, part of Bashar al-Assad’s regime, was in charge of Adra prison where prisoners were tortured

This article contains descriptions of torture.

A US…

items: This article contains descriptions of torture.

blocks.text: A US federal court in Los Angeles sentenced a former Syrian government official who ran one of the country’s most infamous prisons to 60 years in prison on Thursday – the most significant punishment handed to an official of ousted president Bashar al-Assad’s regime by a foreign court and to a defendant present in person.

Samir Ousman al-Sheikh was the head of the Adra prison, on the outskirts of Damascus, between 2005 and 2008, when he oversaw an underground “punishment wing”, known as “Wing 13”, in which prisoners and regime opponents were interrogated and tortured as he watched through surveillance cameras. A federal jury convicted al-Sheikh last March of having tortured prisoners and then lying about it in US immigration forms.
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” said Hernan D Vera, a US district judge, before delivering the sentence.
Al-Sheikh’s legal team and the justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Following al-Sheikh’s conviction, Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, had said in a statement that the case showed the US “is not a refuge for criminals – especially criminals who engage in the brutality of the kind this defendant inflicted on his victims”.

Al-Sheikh, 73, who also served as governor of Syria’s Deir Ez-Zour province in 2011, at a time of violent regime crackdowns against protesters, moved to the United States in 2020, obtained a green card and applied for US citizenship. He was arrested in July 2024 at Los Angeles international airport on immigration fraud charges and prosecutors later added four-torture related charges.

He is the first al-Assad regime official to go to trial in the US and the highest ranking regime official to be tried anywhere in the world in person. Al-Assad was ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the regime in just 11 days.

Since then, Syria’s new government has held a number of in absentia trials for former regime officials in connection to crimes committed during the country’s years-long civil war, which killed about half a million people and displaced half the country’s prewar population of 23 million. In August, a court sentenced al-Assad and his brother Maher to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the two men have been in Moscow since the regime’s collapse.
Other factions in Syria’s civil war have also been accused of abuse of detainees, including insurgent groups and the US-backed, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces.

During al-Sheikh’s nine-day trial, several victims and witnesses testified. They described guards folding prisoners into car tires, restraining and beating them. Some they said, were cuffed by their wrists to pipes on the ceiling, beaten with cables, and left suspended for extended periods of time.

Others testified that they were placed on a device known as a “magic carpet,” which consisted of two large wooden panels with hinges in the middle onto which guards strapped prisoners, forcing the panels together to cause excruciating pain. One victim recalled al-Sheikh himself stomping on the device. Another testified he was subjected to the “magic carpet” as punishment for writing a letter of support to a political prisoner and also forced to wear a red jumpsuit assigned to prisoners designated for execution, leading him to believe he was going to die.

“[Al-Sheikh] chose to serve the ruthless, repressive Assad regime in Syria throughout his professional life, including for four years as the warden of Syria’s largest prison,” prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “[He] knew that what he was doing was wrong. Nonetheless he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.”

Several victims and witnesses also submitted written and video testimonies to the court ahead of the sentencing, in which they spoke of being haunted and traumatized by their experiences two decades later.
“I still hear the screams of others begging for mercy,” said one of the men, Nidal Shikhani.
“Even though 20 years have passed, I still live in the prison of my memory,” said another, Sultan Abdul Malek. “I suffer from sudden panic attacks and constant anxiety.”

His brother, Khaled Abdul Malek, who was taken to “Wing 13” twice during his four years at Adra prison, spoke of the physical and psychological scars he was left with, including chronic back pain and mobility problems.
“My son Battal asks if he could ride my back and with a heart wrung with pain, I am forced to tell him I [am] no longer strong enough to carry him,” he said.

Several witnesses also submitted testimony on al-Sheikh’s behalf, speaking about his age and frailty as they asked the court for leniency. More than 50 people sent letters of support to the court, describing him as “a person of integrity, compassion, and generosity to his family and community”, his attorneys wrote.

Prosecutors had asked the court for a minimum sentence of 80 years; al-Sheikh’s attorneys had called for a five-year sentence, citing his poor health and noting that he was willing to be deported to Syria.

“Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history – however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ – that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” the defense team wrote in a memo to the court.

“This case sends a message both to the new government of Syria and to other victims that justice is possible,” said Ela Matthews, an attorney at the Center for Justice and Accountability, which represented several victims. “The transitional justice process that is happening in Syria needs to continue to evolve and bring individuals like this to account, but in the US this sends a message that the rule of law is still functioning and that these types of cases are possible.”

articles.title: UN mission notes possible US war crimes in Iran strikes
articles.summary: A United Nations fact-finding mission said it found "reasonable grounds" to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran.

image.caption: According to Iranian authorities, more than 150 people, mainly schoolgirls, died in the strike on Minab [FILE: August 2026]Image: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Experts from the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, commissioned by the UN Human Rights Council, said they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including one that hit a school in the southern Iranian city of Minab.
In a report published Thursday, the experts also accused Iran's theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people.
Established in 2022, the mission is chaired by Bangladeshi jurist Sara Hossain and consists of independent experts.
They were expected to present their findings to the UN Human Rights Council on Monday. The Council is made up of 47 UN member countries.
The mission examined US actions during the Iran war, which started in February, and the Iranian government's response to the nationwide unrest that began in late December.
Although it is not binding, the report contributes to the international evidence gathered about the Iran war and could eventually be used in attempts to bring legal cases to international courts.
How did the US react?
The Pentagon declined to comment on the mission's report. "Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment," it said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the White House issued a strongly worded statement, with spokesperson Anna Kelly saying the UN top human rights body has "accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades."

"The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Kelly said.
US strikes in Minab and Lamerd
In the report, UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe that US forces were responsible for the attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab on February 28.
Iranian officials said that more than 150 people were killed in the attack, including around 120 schoolchildren.
The mission concluded that the attack was indiscriminate, causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure. This amounts to a war crime under international law, according to the report.
UN experts concluded that the school was clearly a civilian facility and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.

They reached a similar conclusion regarding a strike on a sports center in Larned, also on February 28. The report stated that the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school, killing and injuring 22 civilians.
The report concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
In a statement issued in March, US Central Command said that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd that day.
Evidence points to US role in deadly Iran school attack
Crackdown in Iran
The UN probe also found that Iranian authorities carried out widespread and systematic attacks against civilians during the protests that erupted in late December.
These attacks included unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, the report said.
According to human rights groups, bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution.
Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign adversaries, including the US and Israel.

The probe stated that it could not independently verify the death toll, but it believes that the number of deaths and injuries is likely far higher than the official count of 3,038 deaths and 25,000 injuries.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 7:30am

Newly appointed patrolmen and patrolwomen under the PNP's 2026 Regular and Attrition Recruitment Program assemble at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City during their oath-taking and turnover ceremonies on Sept. 16, 2026.
PNP-NCRPO / Released

MANILA, Philippines — The National Capital Region Police Office (PNP-NCRPO) will be placed on full alert status starting Saturday, September 19, in anticipation of protest actions scheduled in connection with the September 21 Martial Law commemoration.

The PNP announced that the transition to full alert status will officially begin at 12 a.m. Saturday, with full deployment of police personnel commencing at 5 p.m. that afternoon, PNP spokesperson Col. Allen Rae Co said.
More than 15,700 personnel will be deployed, according to Co.
He added that the PNP may augment its personnel with forces from Central Luzon, Calabarzon and neighboring regions if necessary.
Asked what gear police would carry, Co said personnel deployed for crowd dispersal management would have standard protective equipment, including helmets, shields and batons.
"Babalik rin po tayo sa main function ng ating kapulisan to ensure the safety of other people and 'yung infrastructures natin," Co said.
(We will also return to the main function of our police force, which is to ensure the safety of the public and our infrastructure.)
"So we have to control pag 'yung crowd natin ay naging unruly," he added. (So we have to maintain control if the crowd becomes unruly.)
The PNP, however, had yet to receive information on any rally permit applications as of Thursday morning.
He added that peaceful assemblies may be held in designated freedom parks even without a permit, subject to existing rules.

articles.title: 'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
articles.summary: Many Nigerians buy their first ever shares - in the oil refinery owned by Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote.

blocks.text: Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."

Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.

"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.

In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.

He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.

Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

articles.title: New wild cat species discovered - with only one known living member
articles.summary: A spotted wildcat long mistaken for relatives has been identified as a new species in Bolivia.

blocks.text: Only one confirmed living member of the species is known - a cat in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.
It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery.
Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual.
It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat.
Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists.
To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens.

"There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.

The study, published in Current Biology, external, uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat (Leopardus tilcayo) of Bolivia.

articles.title: Fact check: Viral Duterte video after ICC appearance is AI-generated
articles.summary: The video appears to show the ex-president thanking supporters and asking for prayers for Sara.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 7:00am

MANILA, Philippines — A viral video supposedly showing former President Rodrigo Duterte thanking his supporters after personally appearing before the International Criminal Court (ICC) is AI-generated.
A TikTok user shared the video on Wednesday, September 16, showing Duterte allegedly thanking his supporters and asking them to include his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, in their prayers.

"Isama ninyo sa inyong mga panalangin ang aking anak na si Inday. Ipagdasal ninyo sana na bigyan siya ng Diyos ng lakas, tapang, at karunungan upang malampasan niya ang lahat ng pagsubok na kanyang kinakaharap ngayon," the AI-generated video of Duterte said.
(Include my daughter Inday in your prayers. Please pray that God gives her the strength, courage and wisdom to overcome all the challenges she is facing.)
The same video was posted earlier by Facebook page Edd AI at around 7:18 p.m., more than two hours before it was shared by the TikTok user at around 9:29 p.m.
The Facebook page also included a disclaimer saying its content was AI-generated, along with the hashtags #aigenerated and #satire.
Duterte appeared in person before the ICC for the first time on September 16 for the third status conference in his case.
He previously appeared before the court via videolink during his initial appearance in March 2025.
— Voiced by Philstar.com / Janelle Liong Script and editing by Philstar.com / Geraldine Santos

articles.title: Far-right German politician heckles Carney with 'U.S.A.' chant before EU address
articles.summary: As Prime Minister Mark Carney approached the podium at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, he was met by a lone heckler with an unexpected chant for a Canadian leader speaking to the EU in France.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney delivers an address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
As Prime Minister Mark Carney approached the podium at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, he was met by a lone heckler with an unexpected chant for a Canadian leader speaking to the EU in France.
German MEP says chant was meant to address 'elephant in the room'
"U.S.A.! U.S.A.!" German MEP Siegbert Droese called out.
Some in the crowd groaned, then Carney chuckled and carried on with his speech where he called for closer ties between Canada and the EU and an "alliance for the future."
In a statement provided to CBC News, Droese said the chant was his way of "addressing the geopolitical elephant in the room."
‘U.S.A., U.S.A.': German politician chants as Carney speaks to EU Parliament
Droese said Carney's reaction to his callout shows the prime minister "clearly has a sense of humor."

Carney's address to the Parliament in Strasbourg is just another step in a bilateral push for a tightened relationship with the EU and comes just a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants Canada to become the bloc's first "associate member" — a new, and as of yet, undefined title.

items: Read Mark Carney's full speech to the European Parliament
What we know about the proposed partnership between Canada and the EU

blocks.text: "It was an absurd and unrealistic knee-jerk reaction for Ms. von der Leyen to propose an 'associate EU membership' for Canada: a status not provided for in any of the European treaties," Droese wrote in his statement.
Droese is a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been surging in popularity among German voters.

The AfD's domestic policies include proposing large-scale deportations of anyone of non-German heritage and a push for what the party calls a patriotic cultural policy to cut funding for projects not deemed suitably national — such as some Holocaust remembrance programs.
In his statement, Droese called the European Commission president corrupt and suggested she's seeking an agreement with Canada to bypass her "abysmal" relations with the U.S.
Droese ended his statement by saying there is a "certain irony in the fact that the six letters 'USA! USA!' were enough" to trigger a reaction.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: YouTube star Ms Rachel to match Macklemore’s $1m Palestine aid donation
articles.summary:
Educator talks of ‘moral obligation’ and urges ‘every wealthy white celebrity’ to make similar donation

YouTube star

blocks.text: YouTube star Ms Rachel has said she is matching rapper Macklemore’s $1m donation to organizations supporting Palestinians, calling on other public figures to follow suit.

Macklemore, who was fired as the opening act on Ed Sheeran’s tour after saying “Free Palestine” on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, pledged to donate the entirety of his earnings from Sheeran’s tour to several organizations focused on the Palestinian people.
Ms Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote on Instagram: “Over 20,000 precious Palestinian children have been killed, and children continue to be killed every day.”
Accurso said her donation would go to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund.
“We have a moral obligation to use our privilege and platforms to protect children and human rights,” she wrote.

Accurso, a children’s entertainer with over 21 million YouTube subscribers, has been vocal about the hardships Gaza’s young people face amid the war with Israel. She encouraged “every wealthy white celebrity” to match her donation.
Accurso is the latest public figure to back Macklemore, after he was dropped from Sheeran’s Loop tour for remarks he made at a 4 September concert about the plight of the Palestinian people.
“Free Palestine! I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” he said during a two-minute speech.

Macklemore’s words prompted a flurry of criticism from Israel-aligned groups. The singer Pink also called on Macklemore to be removed from the tour, and referenced a 2014 incident where he wore a costume decried for bearing resemblance to Jewish caricature. Macklemore apologized for the costume at the time.

Pink expanded on her position in an Instagram post, saying she was not speaking on behalf of the Israeli government, but rather wanted to advocate for Jewish concertgoers who may have been alarmed by the rapper’s remarks.

Macklemore directly addressed Jewish audience members at a second tour date on 5 September, saying: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”
Sheeran has maintained the decision to fire Macklemore was led by stadium owners, including Gillette Stadium and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft.

Sheeran wrote on Tuesday on Instagram: “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care. Nor does it mean I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.”
Kraft and Sheeran are both donating $2m each to Palestinian relief funds, Kraft said Wednesday, although it is unclear which organizations their funds will support.
Four supporting acts, among them American singer Finneas and Danish pop band Lukas Graham, have quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.

articles.title: Trump hails 'major progress' in setting up US base in Poland
articles.summary: The location of the permanent US military base in Poland could be announced "very soon," Donald Trump has said. The US president also praised the leadership of his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki.

image.caption: Karol Nawrocki (left) visited the White House last year. During the visit, Trump offered to send more US troops to Poland [FILE: September 3, 2025]Image: Aaron Schwartz/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that significant progress had been made toward establishing a US military base in Poland.
"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
In August, Warsaw revealed that it was in talks with Washington regarding a permanent US military presence in Poland.
"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance," Trump added in a social media post.

His announcement comes despite his administration's launch of a formal review of its military presence in Europe. This has raised fears among allies that the US could reduce its military presence there.
How did Warsaw react?
Nawrocki, who is a conservative ally of the US president, thanked Trump on X, saying Poland was "ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation."
He added, "I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base."

Meanwhile, Zbigniew Bogucki, the head of the Polish president's chancellery, called Trump's announcement "great news for Poland." He also noted that it came on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland.
In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said his country was discussing with the United States the possibility of establishing a permanent US base on its territory.
"We have already completed the initial stage of the process, not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told the public broadcaster TVP.
Can Poland hold NATO’s line against Russia without the US?
Poland secures NATO's eastern flank
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been pushing for a larger allied presence on NATO's eastern flank.
Nearly 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland, a member of both NATO and the EU. However, they are there almost exclusively on a rotational basis.

Poland's proximity to Ukraine and Russia is a key factor in its security strategy. The country allocates approximately 5% of its gross domestic product to defense spending and has been working to increase the United States' military presence.
In the meantime, Washington heavily criticized several European countries for refusing to allow US forces to use NATO bases in its war with Iran.
